articles.title: Trump denies offering Iran sanctions relief, Tehran says ready for talks
articles.body:
Qatari mediators press peace deal between US and Iran
WASHINGTON/CAIRO, Sept 29 - Qatar said on Tuesday it hopes that shuttle diplomacy between Iran and the US can lead to a breakthrough despite US President Donald Trump's denial of media reports that he was willing to ease sanctions and release frozen funds in exchange for Iranian concessions on its nuclear program.
"We are exchanging messages between the parties, and we're working towards establishing a common ground in order to get into a deal that would save all of us from the repercussions of the conflict," Qatari Foreign Ministry spokesperson Majed al-Ansari told reporters.
The US and Iran have failed to find an off-ramp from their war, now in its eighth month. Negotiations appeared to intensify during last week's UN General Assembly meeting in New York, but have so far not yielded any agreement to reopen the Strait of Hormuz.
Doha once again has emerged as would-be peacemaker after previously playing a supporting role in producing the June memorandum of understanding that led to a brief ceasefire. US and Iranian officials spoke separately with Qatari mediators on Monday. It was unclear if another exchange took place on Tuesday.
Trump repeated his position that Iran must not obtain a nuclear weapon and that the war would be over soon.
The conflict has degraded Iran's conventional forces and damaged its already ailing economy, but Tehran has fought back with missile and drone strikes on US allies in the Gulf and by restricting oil tanker traffic in the strategic Strait of Hormuz, which has pushed up world energy prices.
"I don't know if they are going to give up yet but they'll give up," Trump told reporters on Tuesday.
"They are doing very poorly," he added.
On Monday night, Trump took to social media to deny reports by Axios and CNN, citing unidentified US officials, that Trump was willing to give Iran sanctions relief and release frozen Iranian funds as part of a final deal on the condition that Iran showed "concrete progress" on the nuclear issue.
"This is untrue. I offered them NOTHING," Trump wrote on Truth Social.
Trump has cited preventing Tehran from acquiring a nuclear bomb as a central goal of the war, along with ending its ability to attack its neighbors and creating conditions for Iranians to topple their leadership.
Iran does not have nuclear weapons and denies it wants to develop them, but argues it has the right to a nuclear program for civilian purposes.
Iranian President Masoud Pezeshkian, in an interview with the CBS show "Face the Nation" that aired on Sunday, said Tehran was ready for talks on its nuclear program and other issues, but would not accept "bullying or coercion."
IRANIAN PEACE PROPOSAL
At the United Nations General Assembly last week, Iran floated a peace proposal that would trigger a seven-day countdown to reopening the strait and a pause in fighting.
Trump on Saturday rejected the plan although Iranian Foreign Minister Abbas Araqchi said on Sunday that Washington had not officially relayed a US rejection through mediators.
The war has killed thousands of people and severely disrupted global energy supplies, fueling inflation.
Saudi Arabia, the largest of the Gulf states, was drawn deeper into the war this month as Iranian-aligned Houthi fighters advanced in Yemen, routing forces of the Saudi-backed government and threatening Saudi oil exports through the Red Sea.
Oil prices settled 2.5% lower on Tuesday as investors focused on signs of recovering crude exports from the Middle East, but prices were still on track for monthly gains on lingering concern about supply disruptions.
The US government on Tuesday offered to loan energy companies up to 40 million barrels of oil from the Strategic Petroleum Reserve, the last US batch of crude from a global deal to unleash reserves in the wake of the Iran war.
The United States also stepped up its economic pressure on Iran, sanctioning 10 individuals and entities, including some based in China, Hong Kong and Pakistan, saying they helped Iran procure weapons and components. REUTERS

articles.title: Why Gaza Flotilla's Thiago Ávila is running for Brazil Congress
articles.body:
Breadcrumb
'We must fight imperialism': Global Sumud Flotilla's Thiago Ávila takes his fight to Brazil's Congress
For more than two decades, Brazilian socio-environmentalist and Palestine solidarity activist Thiago Ávila has campaigned against what he describes as imperialism, colonialism and the exploitation of people and nature.
Now, after years of activism and high-profile participation in Gaza-bound flotillas, he is taking that political struggle into Brazil's electoral arena.
A member of the Global Sumud Flotilla's steering committee, Ávila has helped organise a movement that expanded from more than 40 vessels in 2025 to more than 70 by May 2026, bringing together hundreds of activists from around the world.
He was also among those detained after the flotilla was illegally intercepted by Israeli forces near Crete on April 30, 2026. Along with Spanish-Swedish activist Saif Abukeshek, he was held without formal charges at the Shikma facility in Ashkelon and deported on May 10, 2026, following international pressure and a hunger strike.
Now, Ávila is running for a seat in Brazil’s Chamber of Deputies with the green party REDE in São Paulo.
He says his potential term would bring his activism into parliament, with a particular focus on challenging what he describes as Israeli and Zionist influence over Brazilian policy.
"We believe that our candidacy and possible future term can accomplish an even more expressive role in the struggle for the Palestinian cause, in the fight against imperialism and colonialism," Ávila tells The New Arab.
"One of our key proposals is the rupture of all relations [with Israel]," he continues.
"We intend to establish a term that is vigilant to combat the Zionism lobby in our country, in our political process, and most importantly, in our elections. We are aware that Zionism uses scrutiny times to infiltrate, and that Brazil unfortunately has given in many ways, mostly associated with far-right-wing politicians."
Foreign influence in Brazilian politics
His remarks come days after ABIN, the Brazilian Intelligence Agency, forwarded a report on September 19 to the Supreme Electoral Court (TSE), the Presidency of the Republic, and the Ministry of Justice, pointing to the "risk of influence and interference from the United States of America in the upcoming Brazilian electoral process."
The information was released by Folha de S.Paulo and confirmed by O GLOBO. The report comes amid a wider pattern of closer US-Israeli alignment across Latin America, including the creation of the 'Shield of the Americas', a coalition of 18 Latin American countries plus the United States, which excludes Brazil's Lula and Mexico’s Claudia Sheinbaum.
The shift has also been reflected in relations between Israel and governments across the region.
Argentina's president Javier Milei has praised Benjamin Netanyahu and co-signed the 'Isaac Accords', a branch of the Abraham Accords aimed at furthering public diplomacy and cooperation between Israel and Latin American countries.
In Brazil, congresswoman Tabata Amaral of the Brazilian Socialist Party (PSB-SP) registered bill 1424/26, which supposedly criminalises anti-semitism and includes criticism of Israel as an anti-semitic practice, despite anti-semitism already being a crime in Brazil since 1988.
On September 21, President Lula told CNN anchor Christiane Amanpour that he was "deeply concerned" about possible interference from the United States in Brazil's democratic election process.
As a counterpoint, the United States spokesperson, Amanda Robertson, denied that the United States or its allies had meddled in Brazilian democracy.
Brazilian Zionist backlash
Political candidates who publicly support Palestine and oppose Israel's genocide in Gaza, like Thiago, are commonly attacked by local Zionist organisations.
These include StandWithUs Brazil and the Brazilian Israelite Confederation (CONIB). Journalist Caio Blinder and academic Samuel Feldberg, who are linked to these organisations, have publicly described Ávila as a "professional activist" whose advocacy is motivated by the pursuit of publicity and political gain.
"This sort of attack is not exclusive to Brazil or to me," Ávila explains.
"They attack all those who report on what is done in Palestine, who report on the genocide, and who report on Zionist infiltration in a wide range of countries — similarly how they attacked United Nations Special Rapporteur on the Occupied Palestinian Territories, Francesca Albanese, environmental activist Greta Thunberg, and other prominent figures in the debate for Palestinian liberation," he adds.
"I treat these attacks as part of the process. Threats against me and other advocates have increased dramatically, and our democracy has largely deteriorated due to the influence of Trump and Netanyahu. This is evident in the growing number of far-right leaders occupying positions of power. We must confront these hateful ideologies with all our capacity."
Pathway as a social-environmentalist
Despite support from a significant portion of the Brazilian-Palestinian community and his role in past flotillas to Gaza, Ávila rejects claims that his advocacy for Palestine is motivated by political gain.
He says that, in the electoral process, voters will primarily consider his work as a social-environmentalist rather than his activism in defence of the Palestinian people.
He also adds that his candidacy rests on the intersection of social justice and environmentalism, and rejects claims of appropriation, pointing to the recognition of his advocacy by Palestinian-Brazilian organisations such as the Palestinian Federation and the Palestinian Front of São Paulo.
"I've been an activist for 22 years now, and for 22 years I have been fighting against exploitation, oppression, and the destruction of nature in order to build a 'well-living' society," Ávila tells The New Arab.
"Both environmental disaster and the war machine that profits from genocide originate in the same system. American imperialism, which provides over 80% of the bombs Israel uses in Gaza, is also involved in environmental damage all around the world," he adds.
"It's not a coincidence that the US military, as an institution, is one of the most prominent sources of pollution for the whole planet," Ávila adds.
"In Brazil, some right-wing state governments, but also certain so-called progressive ones, purchase weapons, espionage software, drones and hypersurveillance technology from Israel's arms industry. These are, logically, tools used for mass exploitation, agricultural deforestation, poaching, mining and many other destructive practices," Ávila tells The New Arab.
"The billionaires who profit from these violations, and those behind the legal frameworks that allow this technology to flow into Brazil and circulate around the globe, are the same."
With elections approaching on October 4, and the country’s sovereignty to choose its own leaders at stake, the open question remains: will Brazilian voters pick their representatives based on the Brazil they want to build for the future, or on the Brazil foreign powers want to build for them?

Hello and welcome to our continuing coverage of the Middle East.

Qatari producer UCC Oil and Gas Holding is in talks for its possible entrance into new fields in Venezuela, the company's head of Upstream, Erik Keskula, said on Tuesday at a conference in Caracas.

The group's ship Aurora found five survivors and the dead bodies in a deflated rubber dinghy in the early hours of Tuesday, the charity said.
It rescued another 23 survivors, including a toddler, from an offshore oil and gas platform where they had taken refuge after the shipwreck.
Those rescued reported that at least six people, including three children, were missing, Sea-Watch said on social media, adding the Aurora was now heading to the Italian island of Lampedusa.
Qatar's interior ministry said it would permit the use of drones in designated areas and within set permitted times starting on Tuesday, according to a statement.
Qatar banned the use, operation and launch of drones nationwide in March in the wake of the regional crisis stemming from the US war on Iran.
An Israeli minister came out in defence of French far-right politician Jordan Bardella on Tuesday, after an investigative website alleged that he had made antisemitic comments in 2013.
Bardella, 31, is the de facto number two to the National Rally's (RN) Marine Le Pen, and is tipped to become prime minister if she is elected France's president next April.
He has rejected the allegations, which were published by the website Mediapart.
Bardella "is one of the clearest voices in Europe against Hamas", Amichai Chikli, Israel's minister for diaspora affairs and combating antisemitism, wrote on X.
"He visited the Nova site and the communities of the Gaza envelope," he added, referring to areas in southern Israel that were ravaged by Hamas during its October 7, 2023 attack that sparked the Gaza war.
"He met survivors. He spoke in Jerusalem against antisemitism."
The minister also posted an image of himself shaking Bardella's hand at the site of the Nova music festival massacre.
Spain is planning to override standard migration procedures and tighten rules on asylum seeking for migrants who arrived in its North African enclave of Ceuta in July's mass crossing, a draft decree seen by Reuters showed, prompting outcry from legal experts and NGOs.
The decree, designed to speed up applications and deportations for the over 10,000 migrants who remain in the tiny territory, would mark a major strategic shift for Spain's leftist, pro-immigration government, a staunch advocate of multilateral rules and institutions, as it struggles to contain the political fallout from the border crisis.
Spain's Interior Ministry declined to comment on the draft.
Palestinian Ambassador to the UK Husam Zomlot has welcomed Labour’s shift on Palestine, telling The New Arab that the government has finally acknowledged that the British public “were right and they were wrong”, as Prime Minister Andy Burnham recommitted the UK to securing a two-state solution.
Burnham, who took office 10 weeks ago, used his conference speech on Tuesday to back the Palestine policy set out by Foreign Secretary Ed Miliband a day earlier, pledging that his government would be “principled in our leadership in securing a two-state solution for Israel and Palestine”.
The remarks followed Miliband’s acknowledgement on Monday that pro-Palestine activists “were right” to protest Israel’s war on Gaza, marking a shift in tone after sustained pressure on Labour over its approach to Israel and Palestine.
On the sidelines of the Labour conference in Liverpool, Zomlot told TNA that Miliband’s speech had “brought a great deal of unity in the party” and expressed hope that the rhetoric would now translate into government policy.
Iraqi fuel trucks loaded gasoline at a Syrian port on Tuesday in a bid to meet surging energy demand as the critical Strait of Hormuz remains closed and mediators work with Iran and the United States to end the war.
The disruption of the strait has sent shock waves through the global economy, prompting countries to scramble for alternatives and sending fuel prices soaring. A fifth of the world’s traded oil and gas transited through the narrow waterway before the war.
Egypt's President El-Sissi has held rare meeting with the country's governors, municipal and village chiefs, commenting on broad range of issues without signaling change in policies, according to state media.
The United States has sanctioned 10 individuals and entities including some based in China, Hong Kong and Pakistan,for helping Iran's Ministry of Defense procure weapons and components, the US Treasury Department said Tuesday.
The sanctions are part of a broader push by the Trump administration to isolate Iran economically and force it to negotiate an end to the US-Iran war that began in February.
“Under Operation Economic Outcast, Treasury will continue to target and disrupt those who provide material, technological, or financial support that allows the Iranian regime to sustain its terrorist enterprise,” Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent said. “Treasury will not tolerate any support to the regime and will continue to identify, expose, and isolate Iran’s enablers.”
Treasury said the sanctions were aimed at degrading Tehran's ability to reconstitute its weapons programs, while increasing the costs for those who supported its procurement efforts.
Britain's counter-terrorism police said on Tuesday that no improvised explosive devices had been found as part of an investigation into a suspected plot targeting a British airbase used by US forces to strike Iran.
Police said a quantity of petrol had been recovered during searches of vehicles at the scene. They added that searches of properties in London had been carried out, and investigative scenes around RAF Fairford were being scaled back and were expected to close completely by Wednesday.
Five men arrested on Sunday remain under investigation after being released on bail, with police saying the decision to release them was an investigative one.
"I understand why this development will have come as a surprise to many, but I'd like to reiterate that it was investigative decision, and one which is grounded in experience and careful consideration of policing powers," Laurence Taylor, head of national counter terrorism policing, said.
An African Union committee urged South Sudan Tuesday to address outstanding "challenges" ahead of its first national election due in December and provide a clear roadmap for a credible vote.
Elections in the world's youngest nation have twice been postponed while the government has failed to implement almost any of the preconditions set out in a 2018 peace agreement that ended a five-year civil war.
"In the interests of national elections that are free, fair and credible, we urge the Government of South Sudan to work with speed to resolve the challenges that remain," said South African President Cyril Ramaphosa, chairman of the AU committee focused on the country.
President Salva Kiir last week dissolved the transitional government in South Sudan, one of the poorest and most corrupt countries in the world, and appointed a caretaker administration ahead of the vote scheduled for December 22.
No voters have been registered while rival armies have not been unified and a long-awaited constitution has not materialised.
The United States has granted Iraqi Airways, the national carrier, a sanctions waiver allowing it to fly to Iran, Iraq's transport ministry said on Tuesday.
Efforts by Prime Minister Ali al-Zaidi and Transport Minister Wahb al-Hasani "successfully obtained a special exemption for Iraqi Airways to operate its flights to the Islamic Republic of Iran", the ministry said in a statement.
A call for military mobilisation by Yemen's government is a sign of growing escalation in the country but has yet to translate into preparations for a new offensive against the Houthis, a leading Yemeni analyst has told The New Arab.
The mobilisation call was issued on Monday by Presidential Leadership Council (PLC) chief Rashad al-Alimi amid heightened tensions with the Houthi movement and signs that Saudi Arabia is taking a more direct role in managing its Yemeni allies.
Al-Alimi called for military forces aligned with the government to increase their readiness and mobilise against the Houthis, who control the capital Sanaa and much of northern and western Yemen.
A powerful Iran-backed militia in Iraq on Monday threatened to bring down the government if it continued to bar Iranian flights from entering the country in line with recent US sanctions.
The Kataib Hezbollah warning came after several countries began restricting Iranian airlines from operating at their airports as sweeping new US sanctions targeting Iran's aviation sector came into force on 23 September.
"We warn Iraqi Prime Minister Ali Falih al-Zaidi and those behind him that any government that does not work in the interests of the people will be brought down by all means," Kataib Hezbollah’s security official Abu Mujhaid al-Assaf wrote in a social media post.
Morocco’s king names Fatima Zahra Mansouri prime minister, the first woman to hold the position in the Muslim country.
North Macedonia said on Tuesday police had busted a "terrorist" cell linked to the Islamic State (IS) group in the capital, seizing automatic rifles and arresting five people, including the alleged ringleader.
In a joint operation with the national security agency, police raided dozens of properties in Skopje on Monday, seizing several guns, including a sniper rifle, ammunition and an IS flag, they said in a statement.
According to police, one of the detainees was a 34-year-old man who was a "member" of IS and had been working in the Balkan country since 2023.
"He indoctrinated young people to further the organisation's objectives, disseminated propaganda material containing extremist and radical content, and acquired and handled firearms," the police said in a statement.
Four others were also arrested in the operation. Prosecutors confirmed charges had been filed against the 34-year-old for "terrorism". He and two others were also charged with dealing illegal weapons.
Turkish authorities have arrested the head of the country’s soccer refereeing body, his deputy and five other people amid efforts to “restore the public trust in football,” the country’s justice minister said on Tuesday.
Akın Gürlek said the investigation was based on “allegations of irregularity” such as “interference in referee classification, assignments, scoring, and appointment processes, as well as rule examinations.”
He didn’t offer more details.
Gürlek said the raids were conducted Tuesday morning in the suspects’ residences, workplaces, and offices.
“We will resolutely continue the fight for clean football to clarify allegations that undermine trust in Turkish football, ensure those responsible are held accountable before the law, and see football defined by the effort, struggle, and sportsmanship displayed on the pitch,” he said.
Israel's defence minister threatened on Tuesday to go after Hamas leaders residing outside Gaza, as the military continues to target Palestinians it says are militants inside the war-ravaged territory.
"Hamas leaders abroad are also in the crosshairs. None of these despicable murderers, who played a central role in the October 7 massacre, should die peacefully in their beds," Israel Katz said in a video statement released by his office, referring to Hamas's 2023 attack that sparked the Gaza war.
De facto Saudi leader Crown Prince Mohammed bin Salman met UAE Vice President Sheikh Mansour bin Zayed Al Nahyan in Riyadh on Tuesday to discuss the situation in the Middle East, Saudi official media reported.
The pair met to "review brotherly bilateral relations and regional developments", the Saudi Press Agency said, adding the sit-down was also attended by Saudi Defence Minister Khalid bin Sal
Iraqi authorities hanged 10 people on Tuesday after they were convicted on "terrorism" charges, security and health officials said.
A health official said the forensics department in Dhi Qar province received the bodies of 10 Iraqis "convicted of terrorism crimes, who were hanged" at Al-Hut prison in the southern city of Nasiriyah. A security source confirmed the executions.

articles.title: UN chief urges US, Russia to negotiate new nuclear treaty amid growing arms risks
articles.body:
Merve Aydogan
29 September 2026•Update: 29 September 2026
UN Secretary-General Antonio Guterres on Tuesday called on the US and Russia to negotiate a successor framework to the New START Treaty, warning that growing nuclear arsenals and weakening safeguards are increasing risks to global security.
"The United States and the Russian Federation must negotiate a successor framework to New START," Guterres said at a UN General Assembly plenary meeting marking the International Day for the Total Elimination of Nuclear Weapons.
The New START Treaty expired earlier this year, leaving, for the first time in more than half a century, no binding limits on strategic nuclear arsenals, according to Guterres.
“This undermines not only the security of those who possess nuclear weapons, but the entire international community," he said.
The New Strategic Arms Reduction Treaty (New START) was signed on April 8, 2010, in Prague by the United States and Russia and entered into force on Feb. 5, 2011. It replaced the 1991 START I treaty, which expired in December 2009, and superseded the 2002 Strategic Offensive Reductions Treaty (SORT), which terminated when New START entered into force, according to the US-based Arms Control Association.
Guterres warned that nuclear arsenals are being expanded and modernized while technological advances are increasing the risks of mistakes and miscalculations.
"Nuclear arsenals are being expanded and modernized. The rattling of nuclear sabers is growing louder. Advances in technology are increasing the odds of mistake and miscalculation," he said.
He also pointed to the failure to reach a substantive consensus of the 11th Review Conference of the Treaty on the Non-Proliferation of Nuclear Weapons and the UN Disarmament Commission's inability to produce substantive recommendations during its latest three-year cycle.
"These are not simply diplomatic disappointments — they are warning signs. And the lights are flashing red," Guterres said.
He said nuclear disarmament is "a binding legal obligation" under the Non-Proliferation Treaty and urged all nuclear-weapon states to reduce the role of nuclear weapons in their security policies through confidence-building measures that ensure transparency.
UN General Assembly President Khalilur Rahman said the global inventory stood at more than 12,000 nuclear warheads as of January 2026.
He said between 2,100 and 2,200 warheads are kept in a state of high operational alert on ballistic missiles capable of being launched at very short notice.
"For the first time since the end of the Cold War, the global stockpile is expected to grow again, as new and more modern warheads enter arsenals faster than retired ones are dismantled," Rahman said.
He said global military expenditure reached nearly $3 trillion in 2025, marking the 11th consecutive annual increase.
"As long as nuclear weapons exist, the danger of their use by design, by accident, or by miscalculation, will remain," Rahman said.
He described the Treaty on the Non-Proliferation of Nuclear Weapons as "the cornerstone" of global efforts to prevent the spread of nuclear weapons and advance nuclear disarmament.
"Let us eliminate the weapons, and let us restore trust by building a world free from nuclear weapons," he said.

articles.title: Pentagon orders more fuzes to turn Hydra rockets into drone killers
articles.body:
The Pentagon has ordered another $52.3 million worth of L3Harris proximity fuzes that turn laser-guided APKWS rockets into drone killers, more than doubling the value of a fuze contract signed just four months ago.
The firm-fixed-price modification, announced by the U.S. Department of War, adds to a contract the Naval Surface Warfare Center Indian Head Division awarded L3Harris Fuzing and Ordnance Systems in late May. The work will be done in Cincinnati, Ohio, and is due to be finished by November 2027. The notice does not say how many fuzes the money buys.
A proximity fuze sets off a warhead when it senses a target nearby, so the rocket does not have to hit a small, fast-moving drone directly to destroy it. L3Harris calls the product its Mechanical Proximity Fuze, also known as the FALCO fuze, after the Fixed Wing, Air Launched, Counter-Unmanned Aircraft Systems Ordnance program. It combines radio-frequency sensor electronics from Technology Service Corporation with an L3Harris safe-and-arm device.
The fuze is fitted to the Advanced Precision Kill Weapon System, or APKWS, a BAE Systems guidance kit that turns ordinary 70 mm (2.75-inch) Hydra rockets into laser-guided weapons. The rockets are far cheaper than air-to-air missiles, and a single F-16 carrying six seven-tube launchers can hold 42 of them.
U.S. Air Force F-16s began using proximity-fuzed APKWS rockets to shoot down Houthi one-way attack drones over the Red Sea in 2024. In testing at Yuma Proving Ground, Arizona, APKWS rockets with the L3Harris fuze destroyed Group 3 drones, the larger class of unmanned aircraft, every time, The Defence Blog reported in May. The same fuze arms rockets fired by L3Harris’ VAMPIRE, a truck-mounted counter-drone launcher that Ukraine has used against Russian drones since 2023.
The original May contract was worth $48.5 million, with options that could raise it to about $98 million and deliveries running through July 2027. L3Harris has said demand is pushing it to increase proximity fuze production sevenfold. Most of the new money, $44.8 million, or 86%, comes from fiscal 2026 Defense-wide operations and maintenance funds. Another $3.8 million comes from fiscal 2025 funds of the same type, which expire at the end of the current fiscal year on Sept. 30, and $3.7 million comes from fiscal 2026 U.S. Army ammunition procurement funds. The notice does not say which units will receive the fuzes.
The Pentagon is also developing a newer air-to-air version of APKWS. In February 2026, the U.S. Air Force awarded BAE Systems a contract worth up to $145 million for an APKWS variant with a long-wave infrared seeker and a proximity-fuzed warhead, which lets the rocket home in on a drone’s heat without a pilot having to keep a laser on the target. That version is planned for U.S. Air Force F-16s and U.S. Navy MH-60 helicopters.

articles.title: Belgium to transfer three F-16s to Ukraine this year, Zelenskiy says
articles.body:
Belgium to transfer three F-16s to Ukraine this year, Zelenskiy says
KYIV, Sept 29 - Belgium will transfer three F-16 fighter jets to Ukraine by the end of the year to help in its war with Russia, Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskiy said on Tuesday.
"There is an important agreement with Belgium on the transfer of three F-16 fighter jets by the end of this year," he wrote on X. "We will work to receive these aircraft through an accelerated procedure."
Zelenskiy said Ukraine had already received "urgent deliveries" of F-16 ammunition from Belgium and Spain, among other countries.
Zelenskiy said later in his nightly video address that Ukraine had received delivery the day before of a "very good" assistance package of a NASAMS air defence system, developed jointly in the US and Norway.
Zelenskiy expressed thanks on social media to the US and Norway.
He also said that talks were proceeding to ensure that Ukraine has a supply of missiles for the Patriot air defence system, which play a critical role in intercepting Russian ballistic missiles.
Zelenskiy said tests were continuing to improve the efficiency of Ukrainian interceptors against Russian jet-powered drones, which fly higher and faster than conventional drones.
Of more than 100 Russian drones deployed on Tuesday, he said, 29 were jet-powered and 18 of those had been downed. REUTERS

articles.title: Putin orders 15,500 more active soldiers as Zelenskyy warns of new North Korean deployment
articles.body:
Russian President Vladimir Putin has ordered the country’s armed forces to add 15,500 active soldiers, according to a presidential decree reported by Reuters.
The expansion will bring the Russian military to around 2.44 million personnel, including 1.55 million active soldiers.
Putin issued a similar decree in August to increase the number of active troops.
On the same day, Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy said he had received information that North Korea was preparing to send another 10,000 soldiers to Russia.
According to Zelenskyy, more than 8,000 North Korean troops are currently in Russia. In August, he said as many as 50,000 North Korean soldiers could eventually be sent to fight alongside Russian forces.
Ukrainian and South Korean intelligence services estimate that North Korea has sent between 14,000 and 15,000 soldiers to Russia since 2024.
Most were deployed to the Kursk region in southwestern Russia, where Ukrainian forces crossed the border in August 2024 and took control of several villages. Russia later sent reinforcements and said in spring 2025 that it had regained full control of the region.
South Korea’s intelligence service, known as NIS, has previously estimated that around 2,000 North Korean soldiers have been killed in the fighting.
Zelenskyy has also called on South Korea to provide Ukraine with air defense support.
In July, South Korea announced a $100 million aid package for Ukraine, equivalent to just under DKK 660 million. The package did not include lethal weapons.

articles.title: Trump says Iran 'will give up,' compares its nuclear ambitions with North Korea
articles.body:
US President Donald Trump said Tuesday that Iran would eventually give up, although he stopped short of predicting when, during remarks at a White House event attended by leading technology executives.
Asked whether Iran was about to concede, Trump replied: "Well, they're doing very poorly. I don't know if they're going to give up yet, but they'll give up, but they're doing very poorly."
He also claimed that more oil had moved through the Strait of Hormuz over the preceding two days than at any previous point in history, including before the war.
Trump made the remarks following a luncheon for tech leaders and artificial intelligence (AI) moguls held in the White House's East Room.
The US president did not provide figures to substantiate the claim. He reiterated that preventing Iran from acquiring a nuclear weapon remained the central objective of the military campaign.
"Iran will not have a nuclear," he said, ending the sentence without completing the phrase.
The remarks came during an event largely devoted to artificial intelligence, which Trump wants to rename "superintelligence," or SI.
Trump: Kim Jong Un 'happens to be a friend of mine'
Trump returned to the nuclear issue when a reporter asked why North Korea had been allowed to develop nuclear weapons while the United States was determined to prevent Iran from obtaining them.
"Ah, that's interesting. You know why? Because you had a different president, and they could have stopped him," Trump replied, blaming his predecessors for failing to halt Pyongyang's nuclear program.
He then spoke about his personal relationship with North Korean leader Kim Jong Un.
"He happens to be a friend of mine, Kim Jong Un. He's a friend of mine. He likes Trump. Doesn't like a lot of other people," Trump said.
"I'm about the only person in the entire world that he likes, and I like him. I get in a lot of heat when I say that."
Trump acknowledged that North Korea possesses a substantial nuclear capability.
"He does have a nuclear capacity, a large nuclear, pretty large nuclear. Not like us, but he has a nuclear capacity," he said.
He again contrasted the situation with his approach to Iran, saying previous presidents "didn't do what I did."
Trump criticizes UK over RAF Fairford suspects
The president also addressed an investigation near RAF Fairford, a British airbase used by US forces, including for operations involving Iran.
Trump said American authorities had been involved in the investigation and criticized the decision to release five arrested men on bail.
"How do you give bail to a terrorist?" he asked, referring to the suspects.
"They put them out on bail. I assume they have them watched closely. But these were serious people, seriously bad people, and they should not have done that."
British counterterrorism police said Tuesday that no improvised explosive devices had been found during the investigation, although petrol had been recovered from vehicles. The five men remain under investigation following their release on bail. Police have said the decision was made as part of their investigative strategy.
Authorities are examining several possible explanations for the incident, including whether individuals may have been acting on behalf of a foreign state. An Iranian connection has not been established, and Iran has denied involvement.
Xi meeting and the race for AI
Trump said his recent meeting with Chinese President Xi Jinping had been discussed with the technology executives gathered at the White House.
"We had a great meeting with President Xi. A lot of respect for President Xi," he said.
The discussion then turned to competition between the United States and China over AI infrastructure.
Trump argued that American companies must be able to build data centers domestically rather than move projects overseas.
"If we're not smart, they'll end up building data centers in other countries, and those other countries will make a fortune, and we won't," he said.
He suggested that China would welcome American investment that failed to materialize in the United States.
"Elon and I sat with President Xi the other day, and he will take every data center that we don't want," Trump said, referring to Elon Musk.
Trump also praised the American technology industry's position in the global AI race.
"Our companies are dominating the world," he said. "They're dominating China. They're dominating everyone. We want to keep it that way."
The White House said following Xi's recent visit that the two countries had agreed to use the term "superintelligence" and establish a dialogue on the technology's risks and benefits.
Musk predicts 'an age of abundance'
Musk was asked what superintelligence could mean for workers concerned that their jobs may disappear.
"I think by far the most likely outcome is an age of abundance, where we don't have just universal basic income. We have universal high income," he said.
Musk argued that advances in robotics and superintelligence could eventually make medical care far more widely available.
Pressed on what people would do without jobs, he said: "Well, jobs are going to change. Jobs have always changed."
He compared the potential transition to the disappearance of jobs once devoted to performing calculations by hand, work that is now done by computers.
Not every executive offered an unqualifiedly optimistic view.
Anthropic CEO Dario Amodei emphasized that AI presents significant risks alongside its benefits.
"I think the technology has very real risks, and you know, the mechanism by which we address those risks is still under discussion," he said.
Meta CEO Mark Zuckerberg described an agreement among industry leaders on internal controls, outside audits and independent reviews by company boards. He characterized the commitments as an initial step rather than a complete solution.
Trump, meanwhile, expressed confidence that the companies had strong incentives to ensure their products were safe.
"If something goes wrong, their companies are at stake," he said. "They're not going to let that happen."
The exchanges illustrated how an event intended to promote America's technological ambitions became a forum for questions extending from AI safety and competition with China to the Iran war and security concerns in Britain.

articles.title: Nearly 200 combat engagements took place at the front — the General Staff reported on the hottest areas
articles.body:
Nearly 200 combat engagements took place at the front — the General Staff reported on the hottest areas
Kyiv • UNN

articles.title: Era of Iraq without US troops begins as combat presence ends
articles.body:
Breadcrumb
End of an era as US-led coalition forces withdraw from Iraq
Baghdad and other Iraqi provinces hosting military bases used by foreign and US forces are entering a new chapter with the end of the "combat and operational presence" of US forces and the international coalition.
Baghdad no longer has any field barracks or combat camps after Lt Gen Abdul Amir Al-Shammari, director of the office of the commander-in-chief of the armed forces and head of the Iraqi government, announced that the Victory military base, located near Baghdad International Airport west of the capital, is now completely free of US personnel as part of the withdrawal of foreign forces from Iraq.
A new framework based on the bilateral security and political relationship between Baghdad and Washington is set to follow after the withdrawal.
Iraq says it will work to cover the shortfall in military aviation capabilities that will follow the departure of the international coalition, stressing that there will be no foreign combat forces or military bases in the country after 30 September.
Years of US forces in Baghdad
For years, the US military and security presence was distributed across strategic sites inside and around Baghdad, including the Victory military base complex, the largest operations management centre near the capital.
Victory housed headquarters for the general staff, reconnaissance centres, and facilities securing air and logistical transport, as well as advisory headquarters in Baghdad's "Green Zone", the government district.
These forces focused on coordination through the Joint Operations Command to protect the area around the US Embassy and nearby institutions.
In Anbar province in western Iraq, Ain al-Asad airbase was a vital artery for air support, radar systems and supplying equipment and support to fronts near Baghdad.
Harir Airbase in Erbil, the centre of the Kurdistan Region in northern Iraq, emerged as a hub for technical support and logistical movements in the north. Its various roles included intelligence gathering, intelligence coordination through unmanned aircraft, providing air cover, training and equipping Iraqi forces, and carrying out targeted strikes against remnants of the Islamic State.
Iraqi government military spokesman Sabah al-Numan announced on Monday, 28 September, that the international coalition forces had begun withdrawing from the base, saying in press statements that the withdrawal would be completed by 30 September.
Under the 2008 security agreement between Baghdad and Washington, US forces completed their full withdrawal from military bases and cities in December 2011.
The final convoys crossed the southern border into Kuwait, with Baghdad announcing at the time that it had taken over the sites and bases from the Americans and established national sovereignty.
But Iraq soon became compelled to submit an official request to Washington for training and air support after Islamic State occupied about 30 per cent of the country in 2014, amid a security and military collapse of the Iraqi army and armed forces that continues to raise questions without answers.
As a result, the US-led international coalition was formed, comprising 89 countries and international organisations such as the European Union and NATO.
US advisory and combat groups returned to scattered bases, including in Baghdad and Anbar.
The role of the international coalition and US forces in the war against Islamic State from 2014 to 2017 contributed to providing air cover and carrying out direct strikes against the group's headquarters and movements, as well as coordination through reconnaissance aircraft, intelligence gathering and identifying field targets, and training Iraqi military forces, equipping them with modern equipment and weapons, and providing advice on managing battles.
The role of Iraqi forces and Popular Mobilisation Forces brigades was to conduct direct ground combat and carry out raids and operations to liberate villages and cities that had been under the group's control.
But the assassination of Jamal Jaafar, known as Abu Mahdi Al-Muhandis, deputy head of the Popular Mobilisation Forces, and Quds Force commander Qassem Soleimani near Baghdad International Airport on 3 January 2020 marked a decisive strategic turning point like the relationship between armed factions close to the "Axis of Resistance" and US forces and the international coalition in Iraq.
These factions chose to apply political pressure and launch continuous and systematic military campaigns.
This translated into parliamentary demands to expel foreign and US forces as "occupiers", alongside moves to launch strikes and attacks against the US Embassy in Baghdad and vital military bases, including "Victory, Asad and Harir", using missiles and drones.
These attacks led to a state of isolation and heightened security precautions inside headquarters and bases.
The movement of US forces in the field was restricted, and Washington was often forced to redeploy its forces and withdraw some personnel from secondary bases, consolidating them in more heavily fortified camps.
The tensions pushed forward negotiations to restructure the military presence and shift it entirely towards an advisory and bilateral framework.
Baghdad and Washington announced the end of combat missions at the end of 2021, with the missions changing from combat to advisory and training roles, without ground combat forces on the ground.
This followed lengthy rounds of dialogue conducted by the Joint Higher Military Committee between the two sides, which established timetables for evacuating sites, dismantling combat infrastructure and returning full management of the airspace and bases to Iraqi military forces.
In this context, Iraqi Security Media Cell chief Lt Gen Saad Maan said the international coalition had handed over all its bases and headquarters to the authorities and that there would be no coalition combat or training forces after the end of this month.
Maan added that Iraqi security forces were ready to take over the security file and capable of managing it after the international coalition withdrawal.
He said in a press statement that "relations with coalition countries after their withdrawal will become bilateral".
Optimism and objections

articles.title: North Korea warns UN of Japan’s ‘attempts at rearmament'
articles.body:
Amir Latif Arain
29 September 2026•Update: 29 September 2026
North Korea warned the UN on Monday of longtime rival Japan's “attempts at rearmament” while emphasizing that multipolarity in international affairs was an “irresistible trend of the times.”
Addressing the 81st session of the UN General Assembly in New York, North Korean Vice Foreign Minister Kim Son-gyong accused Japan of taking advantage of the current volatile international environment.
He said Japan has accelerated its attempts at rearmament with an "unprecedented" commitment, including the revision of its Peace Constitution, the abandonment of its "exclusively defense-oriented policy," the reformation of its military structure and an arms buildup.
"Such actions are casting war clouds over the entire region," Kim warned.
He said that “under the signboard of counterattack capability," Japan has moved ahead with the development and possession of long-range attack weapons that put neighboring countries within striking range.
Condemning recent joint military exercises by the US, Japan and South Korea, Kim accused the United States of conspiring "with its allies to systematically amend and update the anti-North Korea nuclear war scenarios through "provocative war rehearsals of all hues and military build-up."
"The US-Japan-South Korea military alliance, unmistakably aimed at the DPRK, is being evolved by the United States into a more offensive and aggressive military bloc with a nuclear element," he said, referring to the Democratic People's Republic of Korea, North Korea’s official name.
He reiterated that North Korea's nuclear status is "uncompromisingly" fixed and can never be reversed in any circumstances.
"I would like to reiterate the official position of the DPRK government: the status of the Democratic People’s Republic of Korea as a nuclear weapons state that has been uncompromisingly and permanently fixed both physically and legally with absolutely no turning back, can never be reversed in any circumstances or by any means, no matter how hard and loudly the hostile forces may deny in chorus with all sorts of rhetoric," he said.
Kim observed that multilateralism and multipolarization have emerged as an “irresistible aspiration and trend of the times based on justice and equity.“
"Gone are the days when an individual member state unilaterally imposed its will on the rest of the world and dominated the international political arena."
Kim also indirectly described the US-Israeli war on Iran as "state-sponsored terrorism.”
"The new year started with the most despicable, world startling act of state-sponsored terrorism, followed by worldwide outbreaks of other appalling incidents and events," he said.
Urging the UN to firmly secure its authority and future by promoting equality and cooperation among sovereign states, Kim said the world body should no longer be misused for the sinister political purposes of ''specific forces.''
He said the effects of a disaster-prone abnormal climate have given rise to a succession of extreme high temperatures, droughts, heavy rains and floods in many countries and regions, seriously threatening the survival of mankind.
This, coupled with the spread of communicable diseases and hikes in oil prices, worsened the socio-economic crisis, he added.

articles.title: UAE vice president visits Saudi Arabia in first visit since rift
articles.body:
Breadcrumb
UAE vice president visits Saudi Arabia in first visit since rift
UAE Vice President Sheikh Mansour bin Zayed Al Nahyan visited Saudi Arabia on Tuesday and met with the Saudi Crown Prince Mohammed bin Salman and the kingdom's defence minister, the first visit by a senior UAE official to the kingdom since a deep rift emerged between the two Gulf powers last year.
The visit, following an invitation by Saudi Defence Minister Prince Khalid bin Salman, occurred as Riyadh faces increasing pressure from the Iran-backed Houthis, who have for weeks fired salvos of missiles and drones at the kingdom.
Saudi Arabia has been trying to rally international support to confront the Houthis, but it was not immediately clear if that request extended to the UAE.
The United Arab Emirates was once Saudi Arabia’s main regional partner in the war against the Houthis.
Sheikh Mansour and Prince Khalid discussed topics of mutual interest and ways to enhance cooperation and coordination between the two countries, according to a post by the Saudi defence ministry on X.
Sheikh Mansour, in a separate meeting with Saudi Crown Prince Mohammed bin Salman on Tuesday, reviewed the "fraternal relations" between the two countries and developments in the region, the Saudi state news agency reported.
The UAE and Saudi Arabia's years-long disagreements over everything from geopolitics to oil policy came out into the open in December when an advance by a UAE-backed southern Yemeni separatist group brought it close to Saudi borders.
Saudi Arabia condemned the UAE’s involvement and carried out an airstrike on a UAE-linked weapons shipment at the port of Mukalla in Yemen.
The UAE then announced it had withdrawn all its forces from Yemen but tensions have remained.
Yemen has been caught in a 12-year-long civil war since the Houthis seized the capital Sanaa, prompting a Saudi-led military intervention.

articles.title: Ukraine’s F-16s have downed over 3,150 Russian targets
articles.body:
- Ukrainian F-16 pilots have shot down more than 3,150 aerial targets, including 666 cruise missiles and about 2,500 drones, Ukraine's Air Force commander said.
- Ukrainian officials and Lockheed Martin discussed a possible move to the newer F-16 Block 70/72.
Ukraine’s F-16 pilots have shot down more than 3,150 Russian aerial targets, including 666 cruise missiles and about 2,500 drones, the commander of Ukraine’s Air Force said during a meeting with Lockheed Martin.
Lt. Gen. Anatolii Kryvonozhko gave the figures when a Ukrainian Air Force delegation he led met with representatives of the U.S. company, the Air Force said. He said Ukrainian F-16s have also flown more than 650 strikes against Russian ground targets. Kryvonozhko said the pilots are getting the most out of the jets despite a limited supply of weapons, using several different types of munitions.
The Ukrainian Air Force did not say when or where the meeting took place, or over what period the kills were counted.
Conor McGuire, who leads F-16 capability development at Lockheed Martin, praised how Ukrainian pilots and ground crews have operated and fought with the jet, and said the company intends to help Ukraine improve the capabilities of the F-16s it already flies, according to the Air Force. The two sides also discussed the possibility of Ukraine moving to newer versions of the Fighting Falcon, including the F-16 Block 70/72.
The Block 70/72 is the latest production model of the F-16, built by Lockheed Martin in Greenville, South Carolina. It adds an AN/APG-83 active electronically scanned array radar, which can track more targets at longer range than older radars, along with new cockpit displays and a longer structural service life. Ukraine currently flies older F-16s donated by European countries, which were upgraded in the 2000s but were not built new for Ukraine.
The first F-16s arrived in Ukraine in the summer of 2024, supplied by the Netherlands, Denmark, Norway and Belgium. Ukraine has used them mainly to intercept the Russian cruise missiles and Shahed-type attack drones that target its cities and power grid, often firing guns and short-range missiles at drones to save more expensive weapons. Ukraine has also lost several F-16s and pilots in combat and accidents since the jets entered service.
Ukraine is also looking beyond the F-16. In October 2025, it signed a letter of intent with Sweden for up to 150 Saab Gripen E fighters, and in November 2025 it signed a similar agreement with France for up to 100 Rafales. Neither deal has produced deliveries so far.

articles.title: Kazakh leader calls Putin ‘outstanding statesman’ in front of Merz (VIDEO)
articles.body:
Kazakh leader calls Putin ‘outstanding statesman’ in front of Merz (VIDEO)
Russian President Vladimir Putin is an “outstanding statesman” suited to leading a great country such as Russia, Kazakh President Kassym-Jomart Tokayev said during his visit to Germany on Tuesday.
A former Soviet republic, Kazakhstan is one of Russia’s closest partners in Central Asia.
Tokayev met German Chancellor Friedrich Merz in Berlin amid heightened tensions between Germany and Russia over the Ukraine conflict. Germany accused Russia earlier this month of attempting to strike Ukrainian cargo planes with drones at Leipzig/Halle Airport in the German state of Saxony. Moscow rejected the claims as unfounded.
During a joint press conference with Merz, Tokayev said he had “very good relations” with Putin.
“I consider him, one might say, an outstanding statesman. And today I said with a fairly high degree of conviction that President Putin, as a statesman and as a leader, is the most acceptable political figure – strange as that may sound to you – for Central Asia, including Kazakhstan, for Europe, and for the entire world,” Tokayev said in Russian.
“I know him very well. He possesses the qualities that are most essential for the leader of a great country with a complicated history and with its own understanding of the strategic goals it faces,” he added.
💥 Der Präsident Kasachstans, Tokajew, demütigte Merz auf der gemeinsamen Pressekonferenz:
"Wladimir Putin, als Führer der Russischen Föderation, ist die akzeptabelste Figur für Europa und die Welt!" pic.twitter.com/FTFhkZMCtl
Tokayev said that although he favors “freezing” the Ukraine conflict, an immediate end to hostilities is “unrealistic under the current circumstances.”
Kiev has rejected Russia’s ceasefire terms, which include the withdrawal of Ukrainian troops from Russian territory in Donbass and an end to Western military aid to Ukraine. Moscow has argued that Ukraine was not negotiating in good faith and accused Kiev’s European backers of trying to sabotage US-mediated talks.
Speaking at a press conference on Tuesday, Merz reiterated that Germany “will make every effort to continue assisting and supporting Ukraine, not only militarily but also politically, financially and economically.”
Russia has condemned what it described as dangerous rhetoric from the West, with Foreign Minister Sergey Lavrov saying last week that the “metastases of an ideology of hatred” were present among EU and NATO members, including Germany.

articles.title: Iran’s Araghchi meets Qatari mediators as US calls for nuclear talks
articles.body:
Iran’s Araghchi meets Qatari mediators as US calls for nuclear talks
Tehran awaits reply on Hormuz plan as a US official says there will be no deal unless nuclear issues are addressed.
Iran’s Foreign Minister Abbas Araghchi has met with Qatari mediators in New York to discuss a proposal to reopen the Strait of Hormuz, while a United States official said there would be no agreement to end the war unless Tehran’s nuclear programme is addressed.
Araghchi told Iranian state media on Monday that the Qatari mediators would carry the ideas discussed at the meeting to the US and that he hoped to receive Washington’s final response by Tuesday.
Recommended Stories
list of 4 items
- list 1 of 4Pezeshkian says Iran ‘no longer trusts talks with Washington’
- list 2 of 4Iran shifts trade north to Caspian Sea as war impairs Strait of Hormuz
- list 3 of 4‘Better deal’: What’s behind Trump’s rejection of Iran’s truce offer?
- list 4 of 4Strait of Hormuz tensions linger as Iran and US move further from a deal
“We talked about ideas and how to find solutions to fulfil Iran’s conditions and how to implement those conditions,” he said. “They had some ideas, and we had a discussion that they will also present to the American side.”
Asked whether he would stay in New York to await the reply, Araghchi said he would fly to Tehran within hours.
“Whenever the Qataris have a response, they know how to get it to us,” he said.
He described the meetings as part of an existing exchange of messages through Qatari and Pakistani mediators, which he said had taken on “a more serious form” since Iran submitted its proposal.
The Iranian plan, announced on Friday at the United Nations General Assembly in New York City, calls on the US to release frozen Iranian funds, lift sanctions and end its naval blockade of Iranian ports. Araghchi said those steps could be completed within four or five days, allowing the strait to reopen and negotiations on a final agreement, including on Iran’s nuclear programme, to begin by the seventh day.
US President Donald Trump, however, rejected the proposal on Saturday, calling it “unacceptable”.
‘Positive, constructive’ talks
The US official, who spoke to Al Jazeera, said indirect discussions were continuing.
The talks were “positive and constructive”, the official said, but stressed there would be no agreement unless Iran’s nuclear programme is addressed. The official said Trump is willing to relieve sanctions and release Iran’s frozen funds in exchange for progress on nuclear issues.
“Iran has indicated they are flexible on the nuclear issues, but the sides still remain apart on the timing of the commitments and who takes which steps first,” the official said.
The official also expressed scepticism of Iran, saying it had broken the memorandum of understanding signed in June by firing on commercial vessels. Tehran denies the accusation and says it was Washington that broke its commitments by failing to halt Israel’s attacks on Lebanon and by seeking to establish alternate shipping routes through the Strait of Hormuz.
Iran had closed the strait, which handled roughly 20 percent of the world’s oil and gas supplies before the war, shortly after the US and Israel launched their offensive on February 28. Iranian attacks on vessels since have sharply curtailed shipping, and oil prices have risen above $100 a barrel.
Even so, crude exports from major Middle East producers rebounded in September to 12.8 million barrels per day, their highest level since the war began, the Reuters news agency reported, citing data from the maritime intelligence firm Kpler.
That is still well below the 18.8 million bpd exported in February.
Some ships have used the US military-supervised route hugging the coast of Oman, travelling at night with tracking systems off and offloading oil to tankers outside the strait. Admiral Brad Cooper, the head of US Central Command, said on Saturday that American forces had assisted 2,000 transits and more than 1 billion barrels of oil in recent months.
The US has also imposed a blockade on Iranian ports and threatened secondary sanctions against airports and companies that do business with Iranian airlines. The United Arab Emirates, Iraq and Oman have already cancelled related flights.
Trump says US will win
Speaking to reporters on Monday, Trump said US officials had also spoken with mediators but insisted that Washington would prevail.
“We’re going to win,” he said. “It’s going to go pretty quickly.” He added that gas prices would fall once the US won the war.
In Tehran, officials struck a defiant tone.
Supreme Leader Mojtaba Khamenei, in a message marking the Iran-Iraq War and Israel’s killing of Hezbollah leader Hassan Nasrallah in 2024, said that the days of foreign domination were over.
“Having suffered painful blows from our valiant combatants and the guardians of the Strait of Hormuz, they [the enemy] dare not venture beyond the Arabian Sea,” Khamenei said in the message carried by Iranian media.
“Whenever they have risked doing so, they have only inflicted harm upon themselves, and the time is fast approaching when the Arabian Sea, too, will be cleared of their presence.”
Major-General Ali Abdollahi, the armed forces chief of staff, meanwhile, warned that Iran and allied forces would deliver a “decisive and devastating response” to any threat against the country.
Rear Admiral Habibollah Sayyari insisted that the Strait of Hormuz remains closed and said Iranian forces were ready to prevent enemy forces from entering the country.

articles.title: Russian ballistic missiles rock Kyiv, disrupt electricity as multi-day Russian attacks on capital continue
articles.body:
Russian ballistic missile attack on Kyiv disrupts electricity, injures 2 as multi-day Russian attacks on capital continue
Editor's note: This is a developing story and is being updated.
Russia attacked Kyiv overnight on Sept. 30 as ballistic missile explosions rocked Ukraine's capital and disrupted electricity in parts of the city, according to Kyiv Independent reporters on the ground.
Kyiv Mayor Vitali Klitschko reported that at least two people have been injured in the attack.
The latest strikes come amid a multi-day attack by Russian forces on the Ukrainian capital.
Over a dozen explosions rocked the city shortly before 3 a.m. local time, journalists on the ground said. The explosions came minutes after Ukraine's Air Force warned ballistic missiles were headed towards the city, as sounds of air defense fire were heard throughout the city. Additional explosions were later heard around 3:40 a.m. local time.
Klitschko said emergency crews are responding to a fire in a residential area in the Sviatoshynskyi district.
A power outage was also reported by journalists on the ground in the city's Pechersk district.
The full extent of the damage caused was not immediately clear.
The latest strikes came as Russia intensifies its attacks on Kyiv since August, relentlessly launching drone attacks, even in daytime, to exhaust the Ukrainian air defense. Recently, Russia has shifted tactics to target the Ukrainian capital with hours-long drone attacks.
Overnight on Sept. 29, multiple missiles and drones struck Kyiv, wounding one person, the State Emergency Service said.

articles.title: Trump denies offering Iran sanctions relief for nuclear concessions
articles.body:
Trump denies offering Iran sanctions relief for nuclear concessions
- US President Donald Trump denied offering Iran sanctions relief or releasing frozen funds in exchange for nuclear concessions, calling such claims "untrue."
- Reports from Axios and CNN suggested Trump was willing to provide relief if Iran showed "concrete progress" on its nuclear programme.
- US and Iranian officials held talks on Sept 28 to try to end a seven-month conflict involving strikes and casualties, amid ongoing disputes over Iran's nuclear activities.
AI generated
WASHINGTON – US President Donald Trump denied on Sept 28 offering Iran sanctions relief and the release of frozen funds in return for nuclear concessions from Tehran.
“This is untrue. I offered them nothing,” Trump wrote on his Truth Social platform, responding to an Axios report citing US officials who said he was willing to give Iran sanctions relief and release Iranian frozen funds in return for “concrete” Iranian steps regarding the nuclear programme.
The Axios report did not identify the US officials.
CNN also reported, citing an unidentified US official, that Trump was willing to give Iran sanctions relief and release frozen funds as part of a final deal on the condition that Iran offered “concrete progress” on the nuclear issue.
Trump has offered shifting goals and timelines for the Iran war that began on Feb 28, when the US and Israel attacked Iran and Tehran responded with its own strikes on Israel and Gulf states that host US bases.
US-Israeli strikes on Iran and Israeli attacks on Lebanon have killed thousands and displaced millions.
US and Iranian officials spoke separately with mediators on Sept 28 as part of a renewed effort to end seven months of war, according to officials from both countries.
Trump has cited weakening Iran’s nuclear capabilities as one of his war objectives.
Iran, which does not have nuclear weapons, denies seeking them. The US is nuclear-armed.
Tehran says it has the right to develop nuclear technology for peaceful purposes as a party to the Nuclear Non-Proliferation Treaty. REUTERS

articles.title: Russian nuclear-capable bomber plane crashes, killing six people
articles.body:
Russian Tu-95 nuclear-capable bomber plane crashes, killing six people
Tu-95 plane crashed during a training flight in an uninhabited area of Amur region, Defence Ministry says.
A Russian military aircraft has crashed in the eastern region of Amur, killing at least six crew members and leaving one hospitalised, according to Russia’s Ministry of Defence.
Russian state media on Tuesday cited the ministry as saying the Tu-95 plane crashed during a training flight in an uninhabited area of Amur, a region bordering China.
The plane was flying without ammunition, according to the TASS state-run news agency.
Interfax news agency quoted Russia’s military as saying that an Aerospace Forces commission had been dispatched “to the crash site to establish all the circumstances of the incident”.
Unverified social media videos of the purported crash aftermath showed large amounts of smoke rising from the burning aircraft.
The Tupolev Tu-95 is a large, Soviet-era bomber aircraft that can carry, launch and deliver nuclear weapons.
It was first flown in 1952 but was only introduced into service in 1956 and remains in use, often by the Russian military in routine military exercises.
This is not the first time aircraft have gone down in Russia’s Far East. In July last year, an Antonov An-24 plane crashed in poor weather conditions on its way to the town of Tynda, killing all 48 people on board.
In August 2021, a Mil Mi-8 crashed in the Kamchatka Peninsula of Russia with 16 people on board, most of whom were tourists.

articles.title: Russia attacked Kyiv with ballistic missiles: fires broke out, and there were problems with electricity and water supplies
articles.body:
Russia attacked Kyiv with ballistic missiles: fires broke out, and there were problems with electricity and water supplies
Kyiv • UNN
On the night of September 30, ballistic missiles attacked Kyiv. Fires have been reported, along with strikes on energy facilities and disruptions to water and electricity supplies.
The enemy attacked Kyiv with ballistic missiles during the night of Wednesday, September 30. This was reported by UNN.
Details
At 2:47 a.m., the Air Force of the Armed Forces of Ukraine (AFU Air Force) warned about the movement of ballistic missiles from the Poltava and Chernihiv regions toward the capital.
Kyiv, take shelter immediately. ... All ballistic missiles are heading toward Kyiv
At around 3:00 a.m., the first explosions rang out in the capital. This information was confirmed by Mayor Vitali Klitschko.
There is a fire in the private residential sector of Kyiv's Sviatoshynskyi District. Emergency services are heading to the scene
In turn, the Kyiv City Military Administration reported that a warehouse building was on fire in Kyiv's Holosiivskyi District.
