articles.title: Syria says arrested Hezbollah-affiliated cell planning attacks
articles.body:
Breadcrumb
Syria says arrested Hezbollah-affiliated cell planning attacks
Syrian authorities said on Tuesday that they had arrested a Hezbollah-affiliated cell in the country's south near the Israeli-occupied Golan Heights, accusing it of planning attacks on unspecified targets.
The new authorities in Damascus, who ousted longtime ruler Bashar al-Assad in 2024, are hostile to the Lebanese militant group, which is a sworn enemy of Israel and fought on Assad's side during the Syrian civil war.
Tuesday's announcement came hours after Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu said there were "indications" that Israel's enemies could try to attack ahead of elections scheduled for late October.
Syrian intelligence services and security forces "thwarted a sabotage plot in the Yarmuk basin in Daraa (province) and arrested a Hezbollah-affiliated cell composed of three individuals", Syrian state television reported, quoting a statement from the internal security forces.
The Yarmuk basin area, where state media has previously reported Israeli incursions and shelling, borders the Israeli-annexed Syrian Golan Heights, as well as Jordan.
"The operation followed careful monitoring of an attempt by the cell to prepare rocket launch platforms with the aim of carrying out attacks to destabilise security and stability," the statement said.
It did not specify the target of the alleged planned attacks and said investigations were ongoing.
Syrian authorities have previously said they dismantled several Hezbollah-linked cells preparing attacks in Syria, accusations the group has denied.
Authorities have also previously announced several seizures of weapons they said were bound for Hezbollah, which lost a key supply route from its backer Iran when Assad was toppled.
In recent weeks, Netanyahu and Israeli Defence Minister Israel Katz have issued repeated warnings to Iran and Hezbollah promising retaliation in case of any attack.
Hezbollah drew Lebanon into the Middle East war in March with rocket fire at Israel, which responded with airstrikes and a ground invasion.
The latest war and a previous round of hostilities with Israel in 2023-2024 have weakened the militant group.
Israel has carried out hundreds of strikes in Syria since Assad's ouster and sent troops into a UN-patrolled buffer zone that had separated Israeli and Syrian forces in the Golan since 1974.
It has also carried out repeated incursions deeper into Syrian territory and has vowed to keep troops in a so-called "security zone" in southern Syria, where it seeks a broader demilitarised area.
Israel captured most of the Golan Heights from Syria in the 1967 Arab-Israeli War and later annexed the areas under its control, a move only recognised by the United States and Colombia.

articles.title: Kataib Hezbollah threatens Iraq govt over Iran airline ban
articles.body:
Breadcrumb
Kataib Hezbollah threatens to bring down Iraqi govt over Iranian airline ban
A powerful Iran-backed militia in Iraq on Monday threatened to bring down the government if it continued to bar Iranian flights from entering the country in line with recent US sanctions.
The Kataib Hezbollah warning came after several countries began restricting Iranian airlines from operating at their airports as sweeping new US sanctions targeting Iran's aviation sector came into force on 23 September.
"We warn Iraqi Prime Minister Ali Falih al-Zaidi and those behind him that any government that does not work in the interests of the people will be brought down by all means," Kataib Hezbollah’s security official Abu Mujhaid al-Assaf wrote in a social media post.
"If the air blockade on Iran continues after the first of next month, our people will take a clear position, which could include closing the border crossings of countries participating in the blockade of the Iranian people," continued al-Assaf. He did not explicitly name the countries he was referring to, leaving it unclear which border crossings he was threatening to close.
All four Iraqi airports that had been operating flights to and from Iran suspended them, significantly expanding restrictions first imposed in Baghdad.
But flights from Iran to and from Najaf have resumed under a US waiver.
Iraq's ambassador to Iran Yasser al-Hajjaj reportedly said on Monday that Iraq had not banned flights but foreign companies were refusing to provide services to Iranian carriers for fear of US sanctions.
The Iraqi state news agency INA said that only Iraqi Airways would now operate flights to and from Najaf.
Iraq is an important market for Iranian airlines, which carry Iranian pilgrims to Shia shrines in Najaf and Karbala, and Iraqi travellers in the opposite direction.
"The Iraqi people will celebrate on the 30th of this month by expelling the occupying US and NATO forces from Iraq," al-Assaf said, referring to the United States completing its military pullout from Iraq after a decades-long presence following the 2003 invasion.
He said the "Islamic Resistance in Iraq" would monitor Iraqi airspace to ensure it was not violated by hostile aircraft, warning: "We will issue a warning first and then shoot them down." He added that the prime minister’s office, under its current leadership, should not become a "cashier" for US violations after 1 October.
Kataib Hezbollah was not officially given seats in al-Zaidi’s cabinet, as al-Zaidi agreed to exclude militia-aligned actors from his government to secure international support and avoid immediate US sanctions, ending months of political stalemate in Iraq.
While Kataib Hezbollah is officially part of Iraq’s state-funded security apparatus through the Popular Mobilisation Forces, it enjoys a large level of autonomy.
Iraq has long played a delicate balancing act in its relations with Washington and Tehran, which both still yield significant political and military influence in the country.
The US backs al-Zaidi’s government and is pressuring it to disarm Iran-backed factions and bring all arms under state control. While most groups have agreed to surrender their weapons and integrate with the state, Kataib Hezbollah has refused to disarm.
When the US-Israel war on Iran broke out, deadly US-Israeli airstrikes hit bases belonging to Iran-backed militias in Iraq which in turn targeted US interests, including Washington’s embassy and bases hosting US forces.

articles.title: Lavrov destroys BBC’s ‘hybrid war’ play (VIDEO)
articles.body:
Lavrov destroys BBC’s ‘hybrid war’ play (VIDEO)
Russian Foreign Minister Sergey Lavrov has treated an accusation from a BBC correspondent with the contempt expected of a veteran diplomat.
The British state broadcaster’s Steve Rosenberg asked Lavrov if he would admit “that Russia is waging a covert hybrid war against European countries?”
“Are you referring to when we destroy the drones and missiles that Britain and continental Europe supply to Ukraine, which are then fired at us?” the Russian foreign minister retorted. “Is that what you mean by hybrid war?”
Rosenberg then dropped his line of questioning and switched to criticizing Russia for its use of “brute force” in Ukraine.
BBC’s Rosenberg: Do you admit that Russia is waging a covert hybrid war against European countries?
Lavrov: Are you referring to when we destroy the drones and missiles that Britain and continental Europe supply to Ukraine, which are then fired at us? Is that what you mean by… pic.twitter.com/XkLe49xcNX
“If you are referring to the destruction of infrastructure used by the [Ukrainian] Nazi regime – with Western support – to wage war against the Russian Federation, then we are resorting to hard power to neutralize this direct threat to us,” Lavrov replied.
Rosenberg’s question to Russia’s top diplomat followed several days of high-pitch war hysteria in the UK press, including a significantly over-reported ‘security incident’ near an RAF base.
European politicians regularly describe drone sightings, fires and accidents at weapons factories, and even natural disasters as examples of a Russian “hybrid war” against the West. The term “hybrid war” is typically used in reporting cases where no hard evidence exists, as was the case when a small quadcopter drone was discovered next to a Ukrainian transport plane at Leipzig Airport in Germany last month.
In the latest such incident, Estonian Foreign Minister Margus Tsahkna blamed Russia on Tuesday for a fire at a drone factory in Tallinn last month. Although the Kremlin has denied any role in the blaze, the UK, France, Latvia, Lithuania, and Sweden all backed Tsahkna’s story and pledged on Tuesday to increase military aid to Kiev.
Amid an upsurge in supposed “hybrid war” incidents, Western military leaders have escalated their war rhetoric, with members of the UK’s Labour and Conservative parties both claiming last week that a military clash with Russia is inevitable, and Spanish media claiming that Italy, France, and Spain are all at risk of a Russian drone attack from the Mediterranean Sea. The latter claim, though widely echoed across the international press, was summarily debunked by senior French and Italian officials.
“We have no intention to fight with Europe…that is utter nonsense,” Lavrov told journalists at the UN General Assembly on Saturday. “But Europe is preparing for war with us, and each day they reaffirm the fact. This could become a self-fulfilling prophecy because they are investing vast amounts of money into weapons production.”

articles.title: Russia warns UK and NATO of nuclear response over Kaliningrad blockade
articles.body:
Russia warned on Tuesday that any attempt to blockade the Kaliningrad Region by the UK or NATO will be met with a response using all means, including nuclear weapons.
In a statement on Telegram, the Russian Embassy in London said this while responding to UK media reports that discussed the possibility of a NATO blockade of Kaliningrad or non-recognition of Russian sovereignty over the region.
“Those advocating plans to blockade Kaliningrad or launch a strike against it should have no illusions about the consequences. Any military action by the UK or NATO against Russian territory will be met with a response using all means available to Russia, including nuclear weapons,” it stressed.
The embassy reiterated that Russia “does not seek confrontation with NATO and Europe and does not intend to attack them,” adding that those who choose to initiate such a conflict “should not be under any illusions” that Russia would respond accordingly.
Russia will use all means to defend its territory
The Kaliningrad Region is a Russian exclave on the Baltic Sea, situated between Poland and Lithuania and separated from mainland Russia by Lithuanian territory.
Last week, in remarks to Anadolu, the Russian Embassy in Paris also commented on what it described as "provocative statements regarding the possibility of NATO forces striking the Kaliningrad region or blocking access to it."
"We wish to emphasise that Russia will use all means at its disposal to defend its territory and that, should any attempt be made to carry out such plans, the retaliation will be inevitable and overwhelming," the embassy said.

articles.body:
“Trump is caught in a quagmire where he can neither negotiate nor fight,” Rezaei said during a Tuesday meeting in Tehran with Shahin Mustafayev, Azerbaijan’s deputy prime minister, accoridng to a report by Press TV about the meeting.
“Iran’s conditions have been conveyed to the United States, but Trump is unable to make a decision, and the United States, out of desperation, has resorted to an air siege in the military war,” he added.

articles.title: US sanctions 10 over allegedly procuring weapons for Iran
articles.body:
US sanctions 10 over allegedly procuring weapons for Iran
WASHINGTON, Sept 29 - The United States has sanctioned 10 individuals and entities, including some based in China, Hong Kong and Pakistan, saying they helped Iran procure weapons and components, the US Treasury Department said Tuesday.
The sanctions are part of the Trump administration's effort to isolate Iran economically and force it to negotiate an end to the US-Iran war that began in February.
Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent said: “Treasury will not tolerate any support to the regime and will continue to identify, expose, and isolate Iran’s enablers.”
Treasury said the sanctions were aimed at degrading Tehran's ability to reconstitute its weapons programs, while increasing the costs for those who supported its procurement efforts.
Those targeted in Tuesday's sanctions announcement include:
• Seyyed Asghar Alizadeh Tabatabai, a Beijing-based representative of Iran's Ministry of Defense and Armed Forces Logistics agency, who Treasury said had coordinated the procurement of finished weapons systems and dual-use components in China on Iran’s behalf.
• Iran-based Kavoshcom Asia R and D Group, which Treasury said had procured electronics including connectors for Iran Aircraft Manufacturing Industrial Company.
• Hong Kong-based EC Mojo Technology Co Limited, which Treasury said had provided electronic components in support of Kavoshcom’s procurement efforts, and EC Mojo's China-based representative Li Fen.
• Pakistan-based Waseem Pasha Tajammal, who serves as chairman of Cavalier Group, a privately owned defense company with locations in Pakistan and internationally.
• Brett Erickson, managing principal with Obsidian Risk Advisors, said the latest sanctions action would do little to impede Iran's ability to launch missiles and drones in the Strait of Hormuz.
• "This is optics management for the Trump administration to claim 'We're hammering them,' when the reality is we're poking them with a toothpick," he said. REUTERS

articles.title: Zelensky, Jewish community leaders commemorate 85th anniversary of Nazi's Babyn Yar WWII massacre
articles.body:
Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelensky attended an annual memorial ceremony to commemorate the tens of thousands of Jews massacred by Nazis at Babyn Yar on Tuesday, which happened 85 years ago on September 29 and 30, 1941.
Several Jewish Ukrainian leaders, including those from the Chabad community, were present at the event. The ceremony was organized by Ukraine's Presidential Office, the Babyn Yar memorial complex, and the Federation of Jewish Communities of Ukraine.
"We must remember the terrible things that happened here many years ago, and now they are happening again, this time at the hands of the Russians," Zelensky said.
"Thank you very much for being with us here today, and thank you for praying for Ukraine, for Ukrainians, for all those who have been killed in Ukraine, for the tragic moments we have endured, and for the Jews who were tortured and murdered. Never again!" Zelensky stated.
Representatives from about 50 countries attended, including Israel's Ambassador to Ukraine Roi Rosenblit. Zelensky thanked the ambassadors and the international community for their "help in fighting against the terrible things the Russians are doing to us, to humanity, and to civilization."
Ukrainian security forces deployed special air-defense systems and snipers positioned around the site due to concerns over a possible attack, particularly threats posed by Russian drones.
Zelensky discusses arrangements for remains of Israeli teen killed in Kyiv to be returned to Israel
While attending, Zelensky discussed Daniel Umansky, an Israeli child who was killed by a Russian drone strike in Kyiv last week, with the FJCU, particularly regarding the arrangements to transport his remains to Israel for burial.
One of the attendees, who has been running Jewish community and educational institutions in Kyiv for nearly 30 years, discussed her grandmother, who was murdered in Babyn Yar.
"Grandmother Sonia was murdered in her fifties. We were unable to find a photograph of her, but we recently located a testimony at Yad Vashem containing her details," Rebbetzin Devorah Leah Levenhartz said.
"It turns out that before her murder, she lived not far from where we ourselves lived, and she now gets to be part of the thriving Jewish community we established...It is almost impossible to comprehend," she added.
"The tragedy of Babyn Yar is an absolutely tragic and bloody example, and today we are meeting on the 85th anniversary of the tragedy of Babyn Yar," Zelensky said in his address.
"This tragedy reminds us how painful it is to lose our family and loved ones, and how the value of human life can be diminished," he added.
"I want to thank you for understanding the value of life. That is, of course, felt especially strongly in Ukraine during this shameful, unprovoked war by Russia against Ukraine, against society, against people, and against life itself," he continued.
What happened in the Babyn Yar Massacre?
On September 29-30, 1941, the Nazis gunned down nearly 34,000 Jews in Babyn Yar in what would later be considered the first massacre of the Jews in the Holocaust.
Babyn Yar is located near Kyiv, which the Nazis took control of on September 19, 1941. A few days later, there was a large explosion at the German command post that killed many German soldiers. The Nazis blamed the explosion on the Jews, intensifying their hatred, so when the SS troops entered Kyiv, the city's Jews were immediately marked for destruction.
Between September 29 and 30, nearly 34,000 Jewish men, women, and children were marched to the ravine of Babyn Yar, stripped and machine-gunned into a mass grave, which was immediately covered, burying some of the victims alive.
The grave was filled with thousands more bodies over the next two years. The total is unclear, but at least 100,000 people were murdered at Babyn Yar over two years. The victims were primarily Jewish, but they also included communists, Soviet prisoners of war, and Roma people.
Despite the tragedy that occurred at Babyn Yar, it took the Soviet Union 25 years to acknowledge the massacre. After trying unsuccessfully to build a sports stadium over the mass grave in 1961, the Soviet Union constructed a small obelisk to stand at the site.
In 1974, a 15-meter memorial statue was erected, but still, there was no hint of the fact that Jews had been murdered at Babyn Yar, as the identification of the victims was vague and did not mention the word 'Jew.'
Only in 1991, 50 years after the massacre, when Ukraine declared independence, was the identity of the victims properly recorded on the memorial, recognizing the massacre of Jews at the site.
Ariella Marsden contributed to this report.

articles.title: Honeywell gets $25.6M for nuclear-tough navigation gyro
articles.body:
- The U.S. Air Force Research Laboratory awarded Honeywell $25.6 million to mature a compact, radiation-hardened strategic gyroscope, with work due by July 2029.
- The contract follows a $41.6 million laboratory award in 2020 for Honeywell to design a Compact Strategic-Grade Gyroscope.
The U.S. Air Force Research Laboratory has awarded Honeywell Aerospace $25.6 million to keep developing a small, radiation-hardened gyroscope accurate enough for “strategic” use, the class of navigation sensor that has to work in space and survive the effects of a nuclear environment.
The cost-plus-fixed-fee contract covers what the Pentagon calls the compact strategic gyroscope maturation project, the U.S. Department of War said. Honeywell will do the work in Clearwater, Florida, and is expected to finish by July 1, 2029. The laboratory’s office at Kirtland Air Force Base, New Mexico, is managing the contract.
Combined with accelerometers in an inertial navigation system, it lets a missile, satellite, ship or aircraft work out where it is and which way it is pointing without GPS or any other outside signal. “Strategic-grade” refers to the most accurate class of these sensors, used where drift has to stay extremely low for long periods, such as in ballistic missile guidance and satellite pointing. Radiation hardening means the sensor and its electronics are built to keep working when hit by the radiation found in space or produced by a nuclear blast.
The notice does not say which weapon or spacecraft the gyroscope is intended for.
The award builds on earlier Air Force Research Laboratory work with the same company. In early 2020, the laboratory’s Space Vehicles Directorate at Kirtland gave Honeywell a $41.6 million contract to design a Compact Strategic-Grade Gyroscope, Military & Aerospace Electronics reported. That five-year effort, carried out at Honeywell’s Phoenix site, called for building and testing four prototypes, refining the design into six strategic-grade units, developing a radiation-hardened custom chip and software for the gyro, flying it on an experimental satellite for a one-year mission in low Earth orbit, and laying out a path toward a gyroscope that could keep operating through the radiation and electromagnetic pulse of nuclear explosions. The earlier contract was scheduled to run through August 2025.
The Department of War did not say how much of the first project’s goals were met or whether the space flight took place. The new work is described as “maturation,” which in defense research usually means taking a design that has been shown to work and making it more reliable, easier to build and closer to use in a real system.
The contract was competitively awarded, and the government received two offers. Only $500,000 in fiscal 2026 research and development money was committed at the time of award, with the rest of the $25.6 million to be added in later years.
Honeywell’s Clearwater site is one of the company’s main centers for navigation and inertial sensor work. The notice did not name the second bidder.

articles.title: British warship hits frigate with live Naval Strike Missile
articles.body:
The Royal Navy used both of its newest anti-ship missiles during a joint US-UK live-fire exercise off the Hebrides that ended with the sinking of the decommissioned American frigate USS Klakring, firing the Naval Strike Missile from HMS Portland and Sea Venom from a Wildcat helicopter of 815 Naval Air Squadron operating from her flight deck.
The round Portland fired carried a warhead and was aimed at a real ship rather than a range target, which the service describes as the first Royal Navy firing of a Naval Strike Missile, although HMS Somerset launched one off Norway in September last year.
Lieutenant Commander Louise Kirkaldy, HMS Portland’s principal warfare officer, said: “The successful firing of Naval Strike Missile marks a significant milestone for the Royal Navy, demonstrating our ability to deliver credible, modern maritime strike capability. This achievement reflects the professionalism, dedication and teamwork of all those involved, whose hard work has ensured we remain ready to meet the challenges of today and tomorrow.”
Petty Officer James Kenyon, an above water warfare specialist aboard the frigate, fired it. “To be involved in such a high-profile exercise is the highlight of my career,” he said. “Being the first person to fire war-shot Naval Strike Missile and achieve a hit is a very proud moment, and one that will stay with me for the rest of my career. This was the culmination of over a year’s effort in planning and bringing the drills into service, and I am glad that I was able to contribute.”
Commander Dafydd Bryden, the ship’s commanding officer, said: “The opportunity to fire anti-ship missiles against a decommissioned warship is an important test of our warfighting capability. This engagement proved the effectiveness of these systems as well as the sailors and aircrew who operate them. We remain ready to fight and win at sea.”
Sea Venom was fired from the Wildcat during the same serial, and Captain Kelechi Ndukwe, commander of Task Force 65, confirmed to journalists that it was the missile’s first live firing since reaching initial operating capability, and that it hit the target. According to the Royal Navy, the helicopter completed the full kill chain by detecting, identifying and striking the target rather than simply releasing the weapon.
Lieutenant Commander Rhydian Edwards, test and evaluation commander at the Maritime Aviation Strike Operational Advantage Group, said: “This was a landmark moment for the Wildcat Force. For the first time we demonstrated the live firing of an operational Sea Venom missile against a representative maritime target. More importantly, we proved our ability to execute the full maritime strike kill chain under realistic operational conditions.
“This was about giving commanders confidence that Wildcat can find, fix and strike maritime targets using Sea Venom as part of a wider task group. The lessons learned from this activity will directly inform future tactics, training and operational capability development, ensuring Maritime Aviation Strike remains ready to fight and win when called upon.”
The Naval Strike Missile was brought into Royal Navy service under an interim arrangement to replace Harpoon, which left service in 2023, and has been fitted to Type 23 frigates and Type 45 destroyers using equipment transferred between hulls as ships enter and leave refit. Built by Kongsberg, the weapon is a sea-skimming missile with a low radar signature and a range well beyond that of the system it replaced, and it can strike land targets as well as ships. The service says it carries an advanced warhead, travels close to supersonic speeds and can reach targets more than 100 miles away while evading detection by skimming the sea, and that it will be complementary to the Future Cruise Anti-Ship Weapon, intended to become the fleet’s premier long-range anti-ship missile aboard the Type 26 and Type 31 frigates through the Mk41 vertical launch system.
Sea Venom, built by MBDA, is the Wildcat’s principal anti-ship weapon and replaced the Sea Skua carried by the Lynx. The Royal Navy describes it as designed to defeat corvette sized vessels or disable frigates, destroyers and other larger ships, with a Wildcat able to carry four at once, and says it can also be used overland against bunkers, buildings and vehicles. Readers will have seen the same missile turn up this week on a very different platform, fitted by STARK to an uncrewed surface vessel built near Plymouth.
The two British weapons were part of a wider engagement in which USS Paul Ignatius demonstrated the maximum damage and range capability of an anti-surface variant of the Standard Missile 6, and the submarine USS Massachusetts engaged the target with the Mark 48 Advanced Capability Torpedo, which delivered the final hit and sank the ship, as we reported.
Weapons were used in order of reach too we understand, with the longest range ordnance going first. Ndukwe said the American side started with the SM-6 before moving in to shorter range systems, a sequence designed to get the most out of the sensors fitted to the hull for battle damage assessment.
Atlantic Thunder 2026 was led by United States Sixth Fleet and drew in forces from five American task forces alongside the Royal Navy, the Royal Air Force and the United States Air Force. Lieutenant Commander Paul Atkins, the United Kingdom lead project officer for the exercise, said: “Atlantic Thunder 26 demonstrated the enduring strength of the UK-US alliance and the close partnership between the Royal Navy and the United States Navy. Operating together in a demanding environment, we showcased our ability to integrate seamlessly, share expertise and deliver a highly capable, interoperable maritime force. Through combined training and operations, we have strengthened our collective warfighting capability, reinforcing our ability to deter potential adversaries and deliver maritime combat power whenever and wherever it is required.”

articles.title: Araghchi’s diplomacy in NY puts war, Hormuz and nuclear rights at center of Iran’s UN outreach
articles.body:
Araghchi’s diplomacy in NY puts war, Hormuz and nuclear rights at center of Iran’s UN outreach
TEHRAN- Iranian Foreign Minister Abbas Araghchi has concluded an intensive round of diplomatic consultations in New York, using the 81st session of the United Nations General Assembly to press Iran’s positions on the war, the Strait of Hormuz, the nuclear issue, international law and the continuation of diplomacy.
Araghchi left New York for Tehran early Tuesday after several days of bilateral and multilateral meetings with foreign ministers, senior officials, United Nations representatives, international organizations, think tanks and media outlets. He also accompanied President Masoud Pezeshkian during parts of the Iranian delegation’s intensive UNGA program.
 
 The diplomatic activity came against the backdrop of the ongoing confrontation between Iran and the United States and Israel, with Tehran seeking to place its account of the conflict, its security concerns and its conditions for a diplomatic settlement before the international community.
Diplomacy amid war
In his assessment of the New York mission, Araghchi said one of Iran’s principal objectives had been to ensure that the Iranian people’s legitimate grievances and suffering were heard internationally, while defending the country’s national interests and demonstrating that Iran remained an active and confident participant in international diplomacy.
He said the large number of meetings requested by other governments demonstrated that Iran had not become diplomatically isolated. Araghchi said many countries had expressed an interest in engaging with Iran and that the meetings provided an opportunity to discuss both bilateral issues and the wider regional crisis.
A central element of the Iranian diplomatic message was the war and its consequences for regional security, particularly the situation surrounding the Strait of Hormuz. Araghchi said Iran had made a deliberate effort to explain its position on the strategic waterway to both the United States and the wider international community.
Hormuz becomes the immediate diplomatic issue
The Strait of Hormuz emerged as the most immediate issue in Araghchi’s consultations.
According to the Iranian foreign minister, Tehran has presented conditions that must be fulfilled before the waterway can be reopened. He described those conditions as fair and reasonable, arguing that if Washington genuinely seeks a negotiated and peaceful solution, Iran has already presented a framework for achieving one.
Araghchi said Iran’s seven-point proposal had been transmitted to Washington through Qatari mediation. Following a fresh meeting with a Qatari mediator in New York, the two sides discussed ideas for meeting Iran’s conditions, with the mediator expected to relay those ideas to the US side and convey Washington’s response back to Tehran.
Araghchi said he expected the process to produce a response soon, while making clear that any subsequent decision would be taken in Tehran. He also stressed that communication through Qatari and Pakistani intermediaries had existed previously but had become more substantive following Iran’s latest proposal.
The significance of the Hormuz issue extends beyond maritime navigation in Tehran’s presentation of the crisis. Iran has linked the reopening of the waterway to broader security conditions, arguing that the issue cannot be separated from the country’s national security and the wider confrontation with Washington.
That position was reiterated by Araghchi after reports emerged suggesting that Tehran might have modified its conditions. He categorically rejected that interpretation, saying there had been “no change” in Iran’s position and that the conditions for reopening the Strait remained clear. He said the immediate issue under discussion was Hormuz and warned against deliberate media speculation about Iranian flexibility.
Tehran presses UN over violations
One of Araghchi’s most consequential meetings was with UN Secretary-General António Guterres on the final day of his New York visit.
Araghchi briefed Guterres on developments in West Asia following US-Israeli military aggression, and criticized the United Nations’ failure to respond adequately to violations of the UN Charter and international law.
He argued that Iran, as a founding member of the United Nations, expected the organization and its member states to respond to blatant breaches of international law, particularly actions involving a permanent member of the Security Council. He called for an explicit condemnation of Washington’s interventionist measures and threats against Iran.
Araghchi also referred to two rounds of US and Israeli attacks on Iran during negotiations in less than a year, as well as the continuation of a naval blockade and “economic terrorism.”
He stressed that Iran would continue to pursue accountability for those responsible for war crimes.
The meeting also covered Iran’s complaint regarding restrictions imposed by the United States on the normal activities of Iran’s UN mission. Araghchi called on the UN Secretary-General to take steps to ensure Washington meets its obligations under the UN Headquarters Agreement.
Nuclear issue remains part of Tehran’s broader diplomatic message
While Hormuz was presented as the immediate issue in the latest mediation effort, Araghchi also reiterated Iran’s positions on its nuclear program and its national rights.
In his meetings during the UNGA, the foreign minister linked the nuclear issue to the broader question of Iran’s rights, national sovereignty and the future of diplomacy. The Iranian delegation’s approach was therefore not limited to seeking a temporary arrangement over maritime traffic but sought to frame any diplomatic process within a wider set of security and political concerns.
This distinction is important in understanding Tehran’s position: Iranian officials have continued to emphasize that diplomacy remains available, while arguing that negotiations must address the consequences of military action, economic pressure and violations of Iran’s sovereign rights.
Outreach to Russia and the Global South
Araghchi’s New York diplomacy also extended beyond the immediate Iran-US dispute.
The Iranian foreign minister held talks with Mali’s Foreign Minister Abdoulaye Diop, where he emphasized Tehran’s interest in strengthening relations with developing countries, particularly African states and members of the Alliance of Sahel States.
Araghchi expressed Iran’s readiness to hold a joint meeting with the three members of the Sahel alliance and reiterated Tehran’s stated support for the independence and national sovereignty of developing countries. He also criticized European interference in the internal affairs of Sahel states.
A similar message emerged from his meeting with Nigerien Foreign Minister Bakary Yaou Sangaré. Araghchi welcomed Niger’s position against the politicized or instrumental use of the International Atomic Energy Agency’s Board of Governors against Iran and discussed expanding bilateral relations and cooperation within the Sahel alliance framework.
Araghchi also met Sri Lankan Foreign Minister Vijitha Herath on the sidelines of the UNGA, as part of a broader series of talks with counterparts from different regions.
A diplomatic message shaped by confrontation
Taken together, Araghchi’s New York meetings reflected an Iranian diplomatic strategy built around three interconnected messages: Tehran says it remains open to diplomacy; it rejects negotiations under coercive conditions; and it intends to link any progress toward de-escalation to concrete security and political arrangements.
The seven-point proposal transmitted through Qatar represents the most immediate channel for testing whether that approach can produce movement, with Tehran awaiting Washington’s response through the mediators. At the same time, Araghchi’s meetings at the United Nations demonstrate that Iran is pursuing a broader diplomatic campaign over the war, international law, the nuclear issue, sanctions and regional security.
For an Iranian diplomatic delegation attending a UN General Assembly held amid an ongoing military confrontation, the New York mission therefore served two purposes simultaneously: defending Iran’s position before the international community and keeping channels for a negotiated settlement open.
Araghchi’s departure from New York does not mark the end of that process. As he emphasized before leaving, the channels through Qatar and other mediators remain available, and any response from Washington is expected to be assessed by Tehran before Iran determines its next step.

articles.title: Lavrov accuses Europe of waging war on Russia
articles.body:
Elena Teslova
29 September 2026•Update: 29 September 2026
European countries are waging a war against Russia, Russian Foreign Minister Sergey Lavrov said Tuesday.
Speaking on the sidelines of the of the Valdai forum in Moscow, Lavrov said European countries are supplying weapons to Ukraine that are being used against Russia.
“This is a war that Europe is waging against us,” Lavrov said, rejecting European accusations that Russia’s strikes on cargo vessels carrying Western weapons to Ukraine amounted to a “hybrid covert war” by Moscow.
Russia's use of force in Ukraine, he said, was strictly self-defense to elimintate threats.
“If you mean the destruction of infrastructure that is being used by the Nazi regime, with Western support, to wage war against the Russian Federation, then we are using force to suppress this direct threat to us,” he said.
US-Russia talks
On plans for talks with the US, he said they will take place soon.
“We agreed with (US Secretary of State) Marco Rubio that this will happen. Experts should coordinate the specific dates and the specific place,” he noted.
Lavrov cited the return of Russian diplomatic property seized by the US as one of the outstanding issues in Moscow-Washington relations.
According to him, Russia received no encouraging signals from the administration of US President Donald Trump regarding its return.
“There have never been any encouraging comments from the Americans, already under the administration of Donald Trump, on this issue,” he said.
Lavrov acknowledged that the US is still seeking to advance its unilateral interests, but said Washington is nevertheless forced to engage with countries including Russia and China.
Berlin scared of 'missing the train'
Commenting on Poland’s plans to produce Patriot missiles and Europe’s involvement in the Ukraine conflict, Lavrov urged European countries to study Russia’s military doctrine.
Turning to his meeting with the German Foreign Minister Johann Wadephul’s on the sidelines of the UN General Assembly in New York, Lavrov said Berlin may be seeking to become involved in efforts to resolve the Ukraine conflict because it does not want to “miss the train.”
“It is difficult for me to judge what Germany is seeking. I think one explanation that is obvious is simply the desire not to miss the train. They believe the train has already gained momentum — I don't know if that's true, it's hard for me to judge, if they mean the Ukrainian crisis,” he said.
Asked about the agenda for his meeting with Wadephul, Lavrov said the German minister spoke about the “militarization of the European Union,” continued calls for NATO to expand and admit Ukraine, and claims that “Russia is an eternal enemy” and that “in three years we will be at war.”
“If such incantations are being voiced, and the goal, as Mr. Wadephul himself announced it, is simply to reproduce these incantations behind closed doors, without the press, so that Russia supposedly understands that this is all really the case — then this is a futile, and I would even say harmful, undertaking,” he said.
Lavrov said it was “very sad” that some EU and NATO officials were effectively acting as “spokesmen” for what he described as the European position.

articles.title: Raytheon expands Sidewinder supplier base in U.S., Europe
articles.body:
The U.S. Navy is paying Raytheon up to $30.2 million to line up additional suppliers for key parts of the AIM-9X Sidewinder air-to-air missile, including the cooling engine for its heat-seeking sensor and its warhead components.
The undefinitized contract modification, announced by the U.S. Department of War, covers engineering work to qualify new manufacturing sources for several AIM-9X components. Naval Air Systems Command at Patuxent River, Maryland, awarded it without competition, and the work is due to be finished in February 2030.
Qualifying a second source means testing and approving another factory to make a part that currently comes from only one supplier, so that production does not stop if that supplier falls behind or shuts down. The notice lists the parts involved: the cryoengine, which cools the missile’s infrared seeker so it can detect a target’s heat; connectors and wiring harnesses; sensor platform and warhead components; components of the optical target detector, which senses when the missile is close enough to its target to detonate; and parts of the inertial measurement unit, which tracks the missile’s movement in flight.
The work will be spread across the United States and Europe. About half, 51%, will take place at Raytheon’s missile plant in Tucson, Arizona. Another 19% is set for Schrobenhausen, Germany, 12% for Anaheim, California, and 8% for Heilbronn, Germany, with smaller shares in Camarillo, California; Delémont, Switzerland; Midland, Ontario; and Logan, Utah.
The modification is a cost-plus-incentive-fee arrangement, meaning the government covers Raytheon’s costs and pays a fee that depends on performance. Because it is undefinitized, work can begin before final prices and terms are agreed, up to a $30.2 million ceiling. The Navy committed $29.6 million in fiscal 2025 weapons procurement funds at the time of award.
The AIM-9X is the latest version of the Sidewinder, a short-range, heat-seeking missile carried by U.S. and allied fighter jets and also fired from the ground by the NASAMS air defense system. The U.S. Navy leads the program jointly with the U.S. Air Force, and more than 35 allied and partner nations use the missile.
In June 2026, the U.S. Navy awarded Raytheon a $1.1 billion contract for more than 1,900 AIM-9X Block II missiles, including 1,653 for U.S. inventories and 336 for foreign customers, with work running through September 2029. That followed another $1.1 billion AIM-9X award in June 2025, then the largest in the program’s history. Raytheon says it is raising AIM-9X production capacity to about 2,500 missiles a year.

articles.title: Israel on alert after Netanyahu attack warning, but IDF reports no specific threat
articles.body:
Despite Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu’s statement that “there are signs that our enemies will try to attack us ahead of the election,” Israel’s defense establishment has not identified an imminent threat. Security officials have long been preparing for scenarios involving escalation and possible Iranian retaliation, which would not necessarily take the form of missile launches. At the same time, Tehran is troubled by the economic pressure it faces and could attack Israel ahead of the U.S. midterm elections in November in an attempt to draw President Donald Trump into negotiations from a position of strength.
According to these assessments, if the Iranians do launch an attack, they could do so shortly before or after Israel’s election. With Tehran seeking to retaliate against Jerusalem, Israel must remain vigilant on all fronts, but there is currently no specific warning or concrete threat.
In an unusual move, a meeting that had been scheduled to take place at the Prime Minister’s Office was moved to another location. Similar steps were taken in the days leading up to and during the war with Iran. However, this was a routine situation assessment attended by members of the inner security Cabinet and senior defense officials, covering several fronts, rather than an emergency meeting. Netanyahu and his military secretary’s security briefing with opposition leader Yair Lapid, meanwhile, was held Tuesday evening at the Prime Minister’s Office.
After the meeting, which lasted about half an hour, Lapid said: “Security threats must be handled professionally and responsibly. Israel’s security and IDF bases are not backdrops for campaign videos. Without going into details, the IDF, Shin Bet and police are prepared for the election, and there is no reason to send the public into a panic. The IDF chief of staff has raised 10 red flags over a shortage of combat troops and attrition in the IDF. If Netanyahu is so concerned about the security situation, he should enlist the 15,000 Haredi men the IDF is lacking.”
Earlier, Lapid and former Prime Minister Naftali Bennett said they had consulted ahead of Lapid’s security briefing with Netanyahu. “Bennett and Lapid stressed the need to discuss the serious and immediate security threat posed by a shortage of 20,000 soldiers and the severe consequences for the reserve forces of the government’s refusal to draft all sectors of Israeli society,” a statement on their behalf said. “They also discussed ways to ensure the integrity of the electoral process and keep political considerations out of security missions.”
No change in the situation assessment
Against the backdrop of the warnings and political statements, Israel’s defense establishment remains on high alert, both defensively and offensively, because of the holiday period and the tense period ahead of the election. However, security officials stress tht there has been no change in the situation assessment in recent days and that, as of Tuesday evening, Israel has no specific, concrete intelligence indicating that hostile actors intend to launch a particular attack.
The defense establishment has been careful to avoid being drawn into the political arena and the exchanges between the parties and has therefore refrained from officially responding to Netanyahu’s statement. In addition, various security officials are exercising caution and prefer not to make statements that could be interpreted as a confrontation with the political leadership.
The IDF stresses that Netanyahu’s statement does not reflect a change in its assessment and that it is not aware of any special preparations or heightened alert beyond what is routinely in place during holidays. Since the ceasefire with Iran, the Israeli Air Force and Military Intelligence Directorate have compiled an updated target bank. At the same time, Israel has maintained closer, more direct coordination than ever with the U.S. military as part of preparations for various defensive and offensive scenarios. The IDF has also recently made operational changes and conducted a series of exercises along Israel’s various borders to ensure an appropriate response in the event of a ground attack.
Despite the general state of vigilance, IDF forces have been scaled back in various sectors. This has included a reduction in forces along the Lebanese border, while the main focus of operations is currently in Judea and Samaria, also known as the West Bank. At bases where the situation assessment permitted it, service members were released for the holiday.
The Home Front Command, meanwhile, has made no changes to instructions for the public and has issued no notice of any development requiring special preparations. The prime minister’s statement did raise public concerns about an imminent attack, but the defense establishment views the situation in considerably less alarming terms. Officials say situation assessments are conducted continuously and evolve daily, with regular intelligence updates on threats across all fronts.
