articles.title: What to Know About the Pentagon Breach Affecting Millions
articles.body:
A reported monthslong breach in the Defense Department’s human resources database exposed personal information of millions of military personnel and those related to them, including their Social Security numbers and job details.
A Pentagon official confirmed to TIME Tuesday that some 2.76 million “living individuals” and 294,000 “deceased individuals” have been affected by the breach at the Defense Manpower Data Center (DMDC).
The breach was first reported by defense-focused news publication Military Times on Thursday, citing a breach notification letter to a person whose information was in the affected files.
It remains unclear what particular files were accessed and who was behind the incident. The Defense Department official told TIME that individuals whose personal information were accessed had been notified by mail.
The length of the breach and the amount of personal information exposed present a security risk for many personnel linked with the department, and some experts say it makes other security compromises, like phishing attempts, easier for bad actors.
What we know about the breach
The DMDC collates personnel, manpower, training, financial, and other data for the Defense Department for healthcare, retirement funding, and other administrative needs. Its website says that based on FY2024 data, it has the records of more than 60 million people—including the military, civilians, contractors, family members, retirees, and veterans.
But the Military Times reviewed a Sept. 18 letter from the DMDC notifying its recipient of a data breach. The letter reportedly said it discovered on July 16 a security vulnerability in the center’s file-sharing system.
The notice reportedly details that between October 2025 and the time of discovery, some “unauthorized users” accessed files on a server containing the personal information. The type of personal information varies from names to dates of birth, contact information, and others.
DMDC then said it updated the file-sharing system to address the vulnerability. The letter reportedly added that there has been no indication of misuse of the recipient’s information.
Not the first hack
The latest incident involving Pentagon data emerged as the FBI confirmed it was looking into criminal hacking group ShinyHunters’s apparent attack on its jobs website. The group claimed to have stolen “very sensitive data” on nearly all agents and job applicants in response to an FBI notice about them issued in May. (ShinyHunters were also behind a high-profile hack in May of education platform Canvas.)
It’s still unclear how massive the previous FBI breach was, but a New York Times analysis found that it may have involved the stealing of home addresses, Social Security numbers, and job assignments, on top of other personally identifiable information. Reuters reported last week that the hackers claimed they have obtained about 2-3 terabytes of data. Some of the data Reuters reviewed also revealed details of assignments to specific field offices, as well as FBI units engaged in high-stakes intelligence, security, or counterespionage work, which risks endangering national security.
In a statement to 404 Media and the Times, the FBI said it was “working around the clock to investigate the cyber incident involving FBIJobs.gov and is in regular communication with anyone who may be impacted—including multiple bureau-wide communications within 24 hours of public reporting.”
The FBI incident also follows a breach that may have exposed more than 153 million driver’s licenses in the U.S. and Canada.
What affected personnel can do
Security experts have previously warned that access to troves of records poses a massive security risk, especially if these fall into the hands of foreign actors.
Justin Sherman, a senior associate at the Center for Strategic and International Studies, wrote about the license data breach earlier this month: “It can be tempting to dismiss the next hack of a database as ‘just another data breach.’... But breaches do not exist in a vacuum.”
The DMDC said in its notice to affected personnel that it was offering year-long credit monitoring and identity-restoration services through IDX, a private firm contracted by the department. The defense official said in a statement to TIME that individuals with questions should contact IDX at https://response.idx.us/DMDC or 1-855-744-4556.
According to the Federal Trade Commission, anyone could place a free credit freeze with each of the three major credit bureaus—Equifax, Experian, and TransUnion.
Active duty personnel and National Guard members could also get free electronic credit monitoring to spot problems that could stem from identity theft.

articles.title: F-47 Maker Boeing Tapped for Navy’s F/A-XX Sixth-Gen Fighter
articles.body:
The Navy has awarded Boeing a contract worth more than $20 billion to build its new carrier-based sixth-generation fighter, the F/A-XX. Boeing is also building the Air Force’s sixth-gen F-47.
“The F/A-XX is a critical pillar in our commitment to maintaining peace through strength,” Michael P. Duffey, the undersecretary of defense for acquisition and sustainment, said in a Sept. 29 release from the Pentagon “F/A-XX will dominate contested airspace, extend operational reach, and deliver a decisive combat advantage for the warfighter. The F/A-XX platform represents a crucial, non-negotiable investment in America’s national security and long-term air combat capabilities.”
The Pentagon release states that the F/A-XX will first augment, and eventually replace, older F/A-18E/F Super Hornets and EA-18G Growlers beginning in the 2030s. It will operate alongside the carrier-based F-35C Joint Strike Fighters, which the Navy and Marine Corps both fly.
The selection ensures Boeing will make two of the three sixth-generation aircraft in development for the U.S. military—the firm won the contract for the Air Force’s sixth-gen fighter program in March 2025 with the F-47. It also represents a loss for Northrop Grumman, the only other company that remained in the running for the Navy’s Next-Generation Air Dominance fighter, and the maker of the Air Force’s B-21 Raider.
“We are joining forces with Boeing to field these capabilities rapidly, ensuring our warfighters possess the lethal and highly networked systems required to deter aggression, project undisputed power, and secure absolute air superiority,” Duffey said.
The Pentagon release said F/A-XX will be able to fly alongside and control semi-autonomous Navy drones known as Collaborative Combat Aircraft.
“This achievement marks a new era for the U.S. Navy,” acting Navy Secretary Hung Cao said. “The sixth-generation fighter is a generational leap in air superiority and will provide the world’s best aviators with unparalleled capabilities to fight, win, and come home safe. We are excited to partner with Boeing, and for our warfighters to continue to dominate the skies and defeat our nation’s enemies.”
Advanced stealth is also considered to be a key attribute of sixth-generation aircraft.
Now-retired Rear Adm. Michael Donnelly, the former director of the Navy’s air warfare division, said at an April 2025 conference that F/A-XX could be the Navy’s last manned fighter.
“It could be our last tactical manned fighter that we operate out of the Navy,” Donnelly said at the Navy League’s Sea Air Space conference in National Harbor, Md. “It will actually be at a point where we are more man-on-the-loop than man-in-the-loop, and be the bridge to fully integrating towards the hybrid air wing [combining piloted aircraft and unmanned platforms] in the future, in the 2040s.”
Donnelly told reporters at that conference that F/A-XX would likely be able to fly more than 25 percent farther than current Navy fighters before needing refueling. The F/A-18 Super Hornet has a roughly 1,275-nautical mile combat range, which is slightly more than the F-35C Joint Strike Fighter’s combat range of more than 1,200 nautical miles.
“That’s a core attribute of the F/A-XX,” Donnelly said in 2025. “It will definitely have longer inherent range, and then with refueling, you could say that’s indefinite, as long as refueling is available.”
Boeing said in a statement that F/A-XX “will revolutionize advancements in open mission systems architecture, advanced mission systems, and operational reach and capacity.”
“It’s an honor to be selected to produce the Navy’s first sixth-generation platform,” Steve Parker, president and chief executive officer of Boeing Defense, Space and Security, said in the company’s own statement. “Backed by decades of work, bolstered by game-changing innovations and solidified by the investments we’ve made in new facilities uniquely suited to build multiple products with next-generation capabilities, our dedicated and talented team is ready to execute this critical program.”
Boeing said technical and program details on the F/A-XX are classified and could not be released.
Longtime defense analyst J.J. Gertler said the Navy’s choice of Boeing could leverage work Boeing is now doing with its F-47 sixth-generation fighter for the Air Force. That connection could accelerate the F/A-XX process and get it into production faster.
“If it’s based on the F-47 or was codeveloped with the F-47, they might be able to put an aircraft in the air very quickly,” Gertler told Air & Space Forces Magazine.
Boeing has invested heavily in building more facilities for advanced aircraft production in St. Louis, Mo., where the F-47 is now in the works, Gertler said.
Boeing is also building F-15EX Eagle II fighters and T-7 Red Hawk trainer jets for the Air Force in St. Louis. Indeed, also on Sept. 29, the Pentagon awarded Boeing a $2.38 billion contract for 22 more F-15EX fighters.
Boeing said construction is still ongoing for its secure manufacturing facility in St. Louis, which will “be part of the world’s most advanced, all-digital aerospace design and manufacturing system.”
“Delivering two advanced fighters in parallel was always our plan, and we invested accordingly,” Parker said. “We are ready and able to build multiple concurrent future combat aircraft franchise programs.”
Gertler said it remains to be seen whether Boeing will be able to follow through on commitments for many critical military aircraft.
“We don’t know how much of [Boeing’s new advanced aircraft facility] is taken up by F-47,” Gertler said. “They’ve got F-15EX numbers expanding. They’ve got T-7 there. Do they have the people to be able to produce this [F/A-XX] aircraft quickly?”

articles.title: US tells Lebanon Hezbollah disarmament efforts 'not enough'
articles.body:
Breadcrumb
US tells Lebanon Hezbollah disarmament efforts 'not enough'
Lebanon has received negative signals from the United States over its efforts to bring Hezbollah's weapons under state control, with Washington warning that Israel intends to continue its military operations in the south, The New Arab has learned.
Lebanese Prime Minister Nawaf Salam received several messages while in New York on the sidelines of the United Nations General Assembly, including warnings from US officials that Israel intends to maintain the security zone it has established in southern Lebanon.
Washington conveyed that Israel would continue its operations "as long as the Lebanese state does not take serious action to disarm Hezbollah", according to information obtained by TNA, and that it remains determined to destroy the group's military infrastructure.
US officials also told Salam that the steps taken by the Lebanese government so far were insufficient and that efforts to bring all weapons under state control must be accelerated.
According to the information obtained by TNA, Washington called for a firmer approach to the issue, warning that the situation could deteriorate further otherwise.
The warnings come as southern Lebanon faces near-daily Israeli escalation, with Israel stepping up its operations and insisting on maintaining the security zone it has established in the south.
Prospects for a solution are meanwhile receding, at least until Israel's parliamentary elections on 27 October.
Salam also received several messages of support, particularly from Arab and European countries, backing the government's decisions and Lebanon's demands for Israel to halt its attacks and withdraw from occupied Lebanese territory.
There was also support for the need to fill any security vacuum in southern Lebanon if the mandate of the United Nations Interim Force in Lebanon (UNIFIL) expires without renewal, with efforts expected to intensify in the coming period to find a solution to the crisis.
Hezbollah sets conditions for weapons talks
Attention is meanwhile turning to Hezbollah and whether the group could enter into a confrontation with Israel, particularly if Israeli military operations intensify.
Such a scenario remains unlikely in the near term, however, as Hezbollah is currently looking to developments between the US and Iran, with Tehran making Lebanon a key issue in its negotiations.
Hezbollah parliamentary sources told The New Arab that the group was "monitoring all developments, and its eyes will remain on the field. Iran remains committed to the Lebanon issue and will not abandon it, which is what should be relied upon rather than direct negotiations with the enemy".
They added that the Lebanese state should return to indirect negotiations with Israel and correct the course of the talks.
The sources said Hezbollah was open to discussing the issue of its weapons domestically and as part of a national defence strategy.
However, they said a complete halt to Israeli attacks and Israel's withdrawal from all Lebanese territory must come first.
Hezbollah Secretary-General Naim Qassem on Sunday renewed his call for Lebanese authorities to end what he described as concessions and review the course of negotiations, calling for direct talks to be suspended in favour of indirect negotiations.
His comments came on the second anniversary of the assassination of former Hezbollah secretary-generals Hassan Nasrallah and Hashem Safieddine.
"Let it be clear, Lebanon without resistance will disappear; the enemy wants all of Lebanon," Qassem said.
"Lebanon can only remain through its liberation and unity and the cooperation of its components. Whoever bets on retaining a part of Lebanon in exchange for abandoning the other part of the land or people is deluded."
Israel steps up attacks on southern Lebanon
Israeli forces carried out a series of attacks on several areas of southern Lebanon in recent hours, including the use of an Apache attack helicopter in a strike for the first time during the latest escalation.
The helicopter struck a commercial centre on the main road between the towns of Shoukine and Mifdoun in the Nabatieh district.
Israeli forces also carried out air strikes on Wadi Zibqin, Talouseh, Mais al-Jabal and the Al-Dabsh area, while artillery fire targeted Wadi Saluki, the outskirts of Kfar Tibnit and Nabatieh al-Fawqa, Al-Mansouri and Wadi Zibqin.
Israeli forces also opened machine-gun fire towards the outskirts of Kfar Shuba in the Azrael area, as well as Sarbin and the Al-Sadana area.
An explosion was also carried out by Israeli forces in Mais al-Jabal, while illumination flares were fired over Hadatha-Haris and Wadi Saluki.
The escalation comes as Israeli media reports suggest southern Lebanon could enter a new phase in the coming days following the completion of what Israel described as "clearing" operations on the Ali al-Taher heights and the destruction of Hezbollah infrastructure in the area.
Direct negotiations remain suspended despite Washington previously announcing that talks would take place in October.

articles.title: Mediators push for US-Iran deal as hurdles remain
articles.body:
Iran's Foreign Minister Abbas Araghchi speaks to the media during the 81st session of the United Nations General Assembly at United Nations headquarters, Friday, Sept. 25, 2026. (AP Photo)
Mediators on Sept. 29 continued to work with Iran and the United States on trying to broker a deal to end the fighting and open the Strait of Hormuz, three regional officials and two U.S. officials told the media, but major hurdles remain between the sides.
The indirect talks come as the conflict, which is entering its eighth month, has caused global economic damage and badly battered Iran. Multiple efforts to allow safe shipping on one of the world’s most crucial waterways have failed.
The officials divulged that the behind-the-scenes efforts continue even after U.S. President Donald Trump initially said he spurned an Iranian proposal to reopen the strait in a week if the U.S. agreed to lift its blockade of Iranian ports, release frozen Iranian assets and waive sanctions on Iranian oil sales, among other conditions.
Iranian Foreign Minister Abbas Araghchi, who stayed in New York after last week’s gathering of world leaders at the U.N. General Assembly, will meet with Qatari mediators on Sept. 28 about the latest discussions, Iranian state media reported Foreign Ministry spokesperson Esmail Baghaei as saying.
Despite Trump’s often bellicose rhetoric, he is open to pursuing a non-military resolution to the conflict if one can be achieved, a senior U.S. official said.
But the Trump administration will not reach a deal with Tehran until nuclear issues are addressed, another U.S. official said.
Trump is willing to grant sanctions relief to Iran, along with the release of some frozen funds, for concrete progress on nuclear issues, and while Iran has indicated it is flexible on nuclear issues, the sides are far apart on timing and which side makes the first moves, the official said.
Two of the regional officials speaking to the Associated Press confirmed that mediators are working with both sides on a proposal that would include reopening the strait and lifting the U.S. blockade and then removing sanctions.
According to the draft text being discussed, the strait would reopen in accordance with a separate deal that Iran has been discussing with Oman, on the other side of the strait, and it would include no tolls, something Tehran has pursued.
That deal seeks to temporarily manage shipping traffic on what was seen as an international waterway before the war.
One regional official said the U.S. is seeking Iranian concessions on nuclear issues that include allowing inspectors to enter the country. Under the memorandum of understanding the two sides signed in June that collapsed within days, Iran’s nuclear program was meant to be discussed over a 60-day period.
The U.S. officials say the United States is skeptical about whether Iran can be persuaded to ultimately reach Trump’s conditions for a deal and would be serious about any promises it makes, especially after it broke the interim deal by firing on commercial ships in the Strait of Hormuz.
U.S. officials feel their position is getting stronger as Tehran feels the impact of sanctions.

articles.title: NATO to strengthen lower-cost counter-drone defenses, Rutte says
articles.body:
Necva Tastan Sevinc
29 September 2026•Update: 29 September 2026
NATO will strengthen lower-cost counter-drone defenses so it does not have to deploy advanced fighter jets against inexpensive threats, Secretary General Mark Rutte said Tuesday.
“We will strengthen cheaper counter-drone defenses so we are not using high-end jets against low-cost threats,” Rutte said at a joint news conference with Lithuanian Prime Minister Mindaugas Sinkevicius at NATO headquarters.
He said repeated drone incidents along the alliance’s eastern flank showed how the threat was evolving. NATO was reinforcing its integrated air and missile defenses through a “multilayered, 360-degree approach” and adapting its posture against drones through initiatives such as Drone Edge, he added.
Rutte cited an incident two weeks ago in which Italian jets deployed by NATO from Lithuania’s Siauliai Air Base shot down a drone that had violated Lithuanian airspace, calling it “collective defense in action.”
Sinkevicius said air defense and preparedness on NATO’s eastern flank were among the main topics of their talks. He said Lithuania remained on track to host a permanently deployed German brigade by the end of 2027.
The two leaders also reaffirmed support for Ukraine. Rutte said Russia’s hostile actions were intended to weaken NATO’s resolve, but pledged that the alliance would “do even more for Ukraine, and not less.”

articles.title: US issues new sanctions over Iran military procurement networks
articles.body:
Rabia İclal Turan
29 September 2026•Update: 29 September 2026
The US Treasury Department on Tuesday sanctioned 10 individuals and entities in multiple jurisdictions that it said procured weapons and weapons components for Iran's Ministry of Defense and Armed Forces Logistics (MODAFL).
"Treasury will not tolerate any support to the regime and will continue to identify, expose, and isolate Iran's enablers," Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent said.
The department said MODAFL is responsible for weapons research, production and acquisition for Iran's armed forces and oversees organizations developing Iran's ballistic missiles and unmanned aerial vehicles (UAVs).
Among those designated is Seyyed Asghar Alizadeh Tabatabai, whom Treasury described as a MODAFL representative in Beijing who "coordinates the procurement of finished weapons systems and dual-use components in China on Iran's behalf."

articles.title: Iran offers up to $40,000 reward to Middle East citizens who capture, kill US soldiers - report
articles.body:
Iran has reportedly offered a reward of up to $40,000 to any citizen who captures or kills an American soldier, according to Iran's Army Spokesperson Mohammad Akraminia in a video circulating on social media on Tuesday.
“It dates back to a time when people, benefactors, wanted to participate in this jihad against the American enemy but lacked the physical capacity to fight,” Akraminia said in the video. “They declared that they could provide financial assistance and make the necessary funds available.”
He claimed that this led to an initiative stipulating that any Iranian citizen who captures or hands over the remains of a US soldier to the authorities would receive a reward of around $20,000.
He said the reward would double to $40,000 if the citizen is a woman.
“Furthermore, I believe that if people from countries in the region were to do the same, that is, succeed in taking down or capturing an American soldier, we could award this prize to them as well,” Akraminia said.
This is not the first time Iran has put out a bounty on US troops. In August, Iranian Army Commander-in-Chief Amir Hatami announced a similar $30,000 reward for citizens who succeed in capturing or killing a US soldier.
IRGC urges Americans to reject Trump’s Iran policy
Earlier on Tuesday, Iran's Revolutionary Guard Corps (IRGC) appealed to US midterm voters to reject US President Donald Trump's policies and accept an offer of peaceful coexistence.
The assertions were made in a 25-page open letter addressed to the American people, urging them to oppose US support for Israel and foreign wars and arguing that Iran and the US could coexist if US policy changed.
The letter accused Trump of concealing the peaceful nature of Iran's nuclear program, which Israel, in particular, sees as an existential threat, and the effectiveness of Tehran's blockade of Gulf oil.
IRGC spokesperson Hossein Mohebbi told reporters he did not expect the letter to affect the US administration's behavior some five weeks before the elections, but that voters might hear the message.
"The American people are not knowledgeable about many developments. We believe if they knew more, they would think differently and take other decisions," he said, adding that Trump is a "big liar."

articles.title: Russia's Kremlin says it does not want Iran to leave nuclear non-proliferation treaty
articles.body:
Russia does not want Iran to quit the nuclear non-proliferation treaty and counts on it remaining a party to the agreement, the Kremlin said on Tuesday.
This follows Iranian Parliament Vice Speaker Ali Nikzad stating that Tehran is considering withdrawing from the NPT, including that the parliament will review a “triple-urgency” motion to do so.
Nikzad reportedly stated that Tehran, which became a party to the treaty in March 1970, has no trust in the International Atomic Energy Agency (IAEA), or IAEA chief Rafael Grossi, because he conducts “merely superficial inspections and submits negative reports against Iran.”
Russia and Iran have close ties under a strategic cooperation treaty.
"Moscow views the NPT as the cornerstone of the nuclear non-proliferation regime and hopes that Tehran remains a responsible party to the treaty," Peskov said, according to Russia's official TASS news agency.
Iran 'has no plans to develop nuclear weapons,' Russia's Peskov says
"Our [Iranian] friends and partners constantly affirm at various levels that Iran is not developing nuclear weapons and has no plans to do so," Peskov added.
"On the contrary, Iran is committed to its obligations under the non-proliferation regime. At the same time, it remains committed to developing such an important economic sector as peaceful nuclear energy within the country," Peskov stated.

articles.title: WATCH: IDF strikes in Gaza, killing Hamas Northern Brigade commander, top military financer
articles.body:
The IDF and Shin Bet (Israel Security Agency) eliminated Hamas Northern Gaza Brigade commander Izz al-Din Beik in a strike in the northern Gaza Strip overnight Tuesday, the military announced on Tuesday.
Beik had served as commander of the brigade since the elimination of his predecessor, Ahmed Ghandour, and had previously served as the brigade’s military intelligence chief, according to the IDF.
In his role, Beik was responsible for managing the activities of Hamas terrorists in northern Gaza and directing efforts to carry out attacks against IDF troops and Israeli civilians, the military said. He was also involved in efforts to rebuild the brigade’s capabilities after they were severely damaged during the war.
The IDF said Beik posed an immediate threat to IDF troops and Israeli civilians and was eliminated in a precise aerial strike.
Prior to the strike, the military said it took steps to mitigate the risk to civilians, including using precise munitions and aerial surveillance.
Predecessor killed shortly after October 7
Ghandour, Beik’s predecessor, was killed in an Israeli strike in November 2023. He had been a member of Hamas’s military council and was responsible for directing the terrorist organization’s activities in northern Gaza. His death was part of a broader operation that targeted senior commanders in Hamas’s Northern Gaza Brigade.
Additionally, the IDF carried out a separate strike against a Hamas financial operative in Gaza City.
The IDF said it eliminated Shadi Abu Hasira, a key money exchanger for Hamas’s military wing, in an aerial strike on Monday.
According to the military, Abu Hasira headed the “Geneva” money exchange network, which transferred tens of millions of shekels in foreign currency to Hamas’s military wing.
The funds were used to finance terrorists, restore military infrastructure, and advance attacks against IDF troops, the IDF said.
Abu Hasira was also involved in commercial activity in the Gaza Strip and managed a company called Gardena Professional, which the military said facilitated his money-transfer operations.
The IDF said Abu Hasira had recently been involved in advancing attacks against IDF troops and Israeli civilians and in efforts to restore Hamas’s capabilities, which the military described as a systematic violation of the ceasefire.
As in the strike targeting Beik, the military said it used precise munitions and aerial surveillance to mitigate harm to civilians before targeting Abu Hasira.

articles.title: Trump considers Russia sanctions relief deal in exchange for prisoner releases - report
articles.body:
US President Donald Trump is considering a deal in which the Kremlin would free some political prisoners in exchange for the US easing sanctions on the Russian economy, The Atlantic reported on Tuesday.
Trump's envoy to Eastern Europe, John Coale, proposed the initiative "a few months ago," and "Trump signed on," the report said.
The initiative, which The Atlantic noted is "still in its early stages," would "promise to advance several of Trump's goals at once."
"It would help reintegrate Russia into the global economy and broaden Trump's talks with the Kremlin beyond the intractable war in Ukraine, which his envoys have failed to end after more than a year of diplomacy...create a path for the US to sign lucrative deals involving Russian oil, diesel, rare earth minerals, and other commodities, [and] as a bonus, the release of prisoners on humanitarian grounds could bolster Trump's case for his long-coveted Nobel Peace Prize," the report said.
However, this approach "is likely to outrage the Ukrainians, Europeans, and even many of Trump's allies on Capitol Hill," the report noted.
This is because "any potential business deal between the US and Russia would risk funneling money to the Russian military even as it continues to terrorize Ukraine and threatens a wider war against US allies in Europe," the report added.
Earlier in September, Trump signed a law co-authored by the late senator Lindsey Graham that authorized the president to "impose severe sanctions on Russia and its trading partners," the report highlighted.
Coale used his successful experience negotiating with Belarus, Lukashenko
Coale, who proposed the strategy, was formerly Trump's envoy to Belarus, Russia's closest ally. During his talks with Belarusian President Alexander Lukashenko, Cole achieved the release of hundreds of political prisoners from Belarusian jails in exchange for easing sanctions and promising to buy potash fertilizer.
Trump has therefore given Cole his "blessing" to do the same with Russian President Vladimir Putin.
Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelensky said during his visit to New York for the United Nations General Assembly that he would try his best to "block" any attempt to lift sanctions on Russia before the war ends, but "it's difficult."
However, Trump's envoys do not see a way to conduct business with Russia without first achieving at least a partial ceasefire in Ukraine, one of the negotiators told The Atlantic.
"Economic ties usually result in normality," Coale told The Atlantic, adding that, in his view, such deals could help bring the Ukraine-Russia War closer to a ceasefire by easing tensions between Russia and the West.
The White House has nominated Coale to serve as the special presidential envoy for hostage affairs, with full ambassadorial rank and privileges, pending Senate confirmation, the report noted.
"The president and his team remain committed to continuing to play a constructive role in ending the war between Russia and Ukraine, and he remains optimistic that we'll ultimately get a peace deal done," a White House official said when asked to comment on Coale's mission.
According to the report, Coale plans to coordinate his efforts with Trump's special envoy Steve Witkoff, who has met with Putin at least seven times since the start of the war.
Most recently, on September 5, Putin expressed gratitude to Witkoff and Jared Kushner for their attempts to negotiate a peace deal following meetings in the Kremlin.
"I'd like to tell you that we find it comfortable to work with you, and, of course, we have a very high level of trust doing this work," Putin told them.

articles.title: US, Iran resume indirect talks through Qatar
articles.body:
Iranian Foreign Minister Abbas Araghchi (C) listens as President of Iran Masoud Pezeshkian speaks during the General Debate of the 81st session of the United Nations General Assembly at United Nations Headquarters in New York, New York, Sept. 23 2026. EPA/SARAH YENESEL
The United States and Iran have resumed indirect contacts through Qatari mediators, with Tehran saying it expects Washington’s formal response as early as Sept. 29 to proposals aimed at reopening the Strait of Hormuz and reviving negotiations.
Iranian Foreign Minister Abbas Araghchi met Qatari mediators in New York on Sept. 28, while U.S. officials held separate contacts with the mediators. No face-to-face meeting between the two sides took place.
“They had ideas, and we discussed how a way could be found to meet Iran’s conditions and how those conditions could be fulfilled,” Araghchi told Iranian reporters.
He said the proposals would now be presented to the U.S. side and Washington’s response relayed back to Tehran.
“I hope this will happen by tomorrow,” he said before leaving New York for Tehran.
The renewed contacts came after U.S. President Donald Trump said he had rejected Iran’s proposal for a seven-day process to reopen the Strait of Hormuz.
Under Tehran’s plan, Washington would take steps including ending its naval blockade, lifting oil sanctions and releasing frozen Iranian assets. Iran would then reopen the strait and resume negotiations on its nuclear program and a broader agreement.
Despite Trump’s rejection, mediated contacts have continued.
A U.S. official described the discussions as positive and constructive but said there would be no agreement unless Iran’s nuclear program was addressed.
Trump on Sept. 28 also denied a report that his administration was prepared to offer sanctions relief and the release of frozen Iranian funds in exchange for nuclear concessions.
“This is untrue. I offered them NOTHING!” Trump wrote on Truth Social.
U.S. Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent, meanwhile, argued that Washington’s economic pressure was pushing Tehran toward negotiations.
Bessent told Fox News that about 15 million barrels of Iranian oil remained in transit, largely to China, and claimed Iran could have “nothing left to trade” within roughly two weeks once those shipments were completed.
He said the pressure campaign was intended to ensure that Tehran complied with the terms of any future agreement.

articles.title: Rutte calls Lithuanian drone shootdown collective defence
articles.body:
The destruction of a drone that violated Lithuanian airspace by Italian jets flying from Šiauliai was collective defence in action, NATO Secretary General Mark Rutte said after meeting the Lithuanian prime minister in Brussels, according to NATO.
Rutte received Mindaugas Sinkevičius at alliance headquarters on Tuesday, the prime minister’s first visit in the role, and said the two had discussed how to keep NATO strong and Lithuania safe. “NATO defends every inch of Allied territory, against any threat, from any direction,” he said, before turning to the aircraft NATO has deployed to the Baltic state. Of the shootdown on 15 September he said: “This is collective defence in action.”
The alliance is strengthening integrated air and missile defence and adapting its posture against drones through a set of initiatives that include one called Drone Edge, according to NATO, which gave no further detail on what that programme covers.
Rutte also referred to the alliance presence in the Baltic Sea and to the Forward Land Forces stationed in Lithuania, welcoming Lithuanian investment in the Rūdninkai training area that will host those troops. On what Lithuania spends on its own defence, the Secretary General was unambiguous. “Lithuania leads by example on defence investment,” he said. “This year, you are expected to reach 5.38% of GDP for core defence spending. Lithuania doesn’t just meet its commitments; it sets the standards.”
That figure sets a marker no other ally is close to matching, since the alliance agreed a headline target of 3.5 per cent of GDP on core defence by 2035, which Wes Streeting restated from the Labour Party conference platform this week as a cast iron British commitment, and Lithuania expects to be spending more than half as much again on top of that this year.
On Ukraine, the Secretary General listed Lithuania’s commitment of at least 0.25 per cent of GDP a year in military assistance, 38 million dollars contributed to the Ukrainian defence industry, and support for energy infrastructure and railway locomotives. “Russia is failing,” he said. “It is failing on the battlefield in Ukraine, and it is failing to undermine our unity and support for Ukraine. Our message to Moscow is clear: we will do even more for Ukraine, not less.”
Šiauliai has hosted NATO’s Baltic Air Policing mission since 2004, with allied detachments rotating through on four-month tours because the three Baltic states operate no fast jets of their own, and Italian aircraft have been among those taking their turn. What has changed is the nature of the work, which for two decades consisted largely of intercepting and escorting Russian aircraft transiting to Kaliningrad rather than engaging anything.
The Forward Land Forces in Lithuania are led by Germany, which has committed to stationing a full brigade in the country, and Rūdninkai to the south of Vilnius is the training area being built out to support it. Britain contributes to the same framework further north, leading the multinational battlegroup in Estonia.
Neither NATO nor the Lithuanian government has attributed the drone shot down on 15 September to any state, and the alliance statement does not say what type it was.

articles.title: UK police release men on bail for airbase incident, US surprised
articles.body:
Breadcrumb
UK police release on bail five men held over airbase incident, 'surprising' the US
British police said Monday five men arrested near an airbase used by the United States were released on bail, as Washington asserted a "foreign actor" was involved in the suspected bomb plot.
US President Donald Trump, speaking in Washington, said he was "surprised that they released them", adding that "I wouldn't have done that".
For his part, US Secretary of State Marco Rubio said Monday that a suspected bomb plot near a UK airbase used by the United States was the work of a "foreign actor."
"It's one that clearly involves the hands of a foreign actor," Rubio told Sean Hannity on broadcaster Fox News in an interview Monday, adding that he would not go into further detail.
The release of the five—all London-based Britons in their mid-20s—came as British Prime Minister Andy Burnham announced an emergency meeting of top officials to ensure they have "the full picture".
Earlier, Iran had denied involvement in any plot to target the Royal Air Force (RAF) Fairford base in Gloucestershire, southwest England, following the security scare there early Sunday.
Here's what we know so far:
Counter-terror probe
UK counter-terror police are leading the investigation after authorities received reports Sunday of three "suspicious" white vans near the airbase, which has been used by the United States to bomb Iran.
Police said in their latest update Monday that the five men held, who all live in inner London boroughs, were being released on bail.
"This does not mean the investigation is over," Assistant Commissioner Laurence Taylor, the head of Counter Terrorism Policing, said, adding the five would be subject to "stringent" bail conditions.
He said officers were "considering this from every possible angle, including that this may be activity committed by proxies, or individuals either knowingly or unknowingly, working on behalf of a foreign state".
The men were arrested on suspicion of explosives offences and "preparation of a terrorist act" under UK anti-terrorism laws, according to police.
They had been travelling in the three suspect vehicles, which have since been subject to "extensive examination, with the support of military assets and forensic experts".
Bomb-disposal team
Authorities have not confirmed details of the threat but bomb-disposal experts were seen working at the scene.
The Daily Mail and Press Association both reported late Monday they understood from sources that tests on materials in the back of the vans established they were "not viable explosives".
A farmer living in the village of Whelford near the airbase said she rang the police after seeing the vans blocking a road and a group of masked men.
The anonymous woman told media on Monday that she believed the police had "dropped the ball" on the threat.
But UK Defence Minister Wes Streeting said the farmer only had a "partial picture".
Iran denies involvement
Trump said on Sunday that Britain and United States had had the suspects "under investigation" for a while and alleged "they were looking to do big damage to our fort".
After hearing news of their bail, Trump said Monday the case "might be" linked to Iran but declined to elaborate.
US Secretary of State Marco Rubio said the incident "clearly involves the hands of a foreign actor", without giving further details.
Iran's embassy in London said on X that it "categorically rejects and strongly condemns" the "unfounded and malicious speculations" that Tehran was involved.
US bombers
Britain gave the United States permission in March to use Fairford for "specific defensive operations into Iran" to destroy Iranian missiles at source.
US bombers and other planes have since been seen taking off and landing from the base—the only one on Britain's mainland used for this purpose.
Residents in the rural Cotswolds area surrounding Fairford said the site, which hosts a range of US military equipment and personnel, had seen increased activity and security in recent months.
Authorities evacuated around 85 households from the village early on Sunday, and they were allowed to return home the next day.
Tehran has previously warned London against allowing its bases to be used by the United States in operations against Iran.
Iranian Foreign Minister Abbas Araghchi has accused London of "putting British lives in danger" by allowing the bases to be used "for aggression against Iran".

articles.title: Trump calls Kim Jong Un his friend, when asked why North Korea can have nuclear bomb
articles.body:
WASHINGTON, September 30. /TASS/. US President Donald Trump has called North Korean leader Kim Jong Un his friend in response to a question why North Korea can have a nuclear weapon, while Iran cannot.
"He happens to be a friend of mine, Kim Jong Un. He's a friend of mine. He likes Trump," he told reporters, adding that he also likes the North Korean leader.
"As long as I'm around, he's going to be fine. Why? Because he respects me and he likes me."
Pyongyang has repeatedly said that North Korea’s nuclear status is irreversible. Foreign Minister Choe Son-hui commenting on a meeting of the heads of the foreign policy departments of the United States, Japan, and South Korea, said that North Korea does not intend to give up its nuclear weapons regardless of the position of the United States and its allies.

articles.title: US senator urges Pentagon chief to review security of military supply chains after F-35 parts diversion
articles.body:
Diyar Güldoğan
30 September 2026•Update: 30 September 2026
US Sen. Tom Cotton called Tuesday on Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth to review the security of military equipment and supplies transported through commercial and contractor-managed supply chains following reports that F-35 components shipped from Australia to the US were diverted to Hong Kong.
In a letter to Hegseth, Cotton raised concerns about the security of US military materiel moving through commercial transportation networks.
He said reports indicated that Lockheed Martin, which manages the F-35 supply chain, transported the components through a commercial carrier and that Chinese authorities had taken possession of the parts and had not returned them.
“We can’t afford for U.S. military equipment to fall into the hands of a foreign adversary because of vulnerabilities in commercial transportation,” Cotton wrote.
Cotton said the Department of Defense relies extensively on contractors and commercial carriers to transport military equipment, replacement parts and other supplies around the world.
"And while I recognize that such arrangements allow for ease and speed of movement, those advantages must not come at the expense of maintaining our military edge," he added.
The senator asked the department to examine five areas of military transportation security.
Among them, Cotton wants the department to review chain-of-custody requirements for equipment and supplies transported by contractors and commercial carriers, as well as the department's ability to track shipments and their routes.
He also requested a review of procedures for approving and reporting changes to shipping routes and the criteria used to determine whether military shipments can pass through foreign jurisdictions.
Finally, Cotton called for safeguards designed to prevent US military materiel from passing through or being diverted to China and other jurisdictions controlled by countries considered adversaries.
Cotton argued that even equipment that is not classified can potentially provide foreign governments with information about US weapons systems, logistics and military readiness.
“Classified and designated sensitive components should receive heightened protections, but all U.S. military material can provide adversaries valuable insight into U.S. weapons systems, logistics, and readiness,” he wrote.

articles.title: Iran rebuffs UAE at UN: Three islands are ‘inseparable parts of Iran’s territory’
articles.body:
Iran rebuffs UAE at UN: Three islands are ‘inseparable parts of Iran’s territory’
TEHRAN — Repeating unfounded claims from the United Nations rostrum “does not alter the reality” that Abu Musa, the Greater Tunb, and the Lesser Tunb remain “inseparable parts of Iran’s territory,” Kazem Gharibabadi, Iran’s Deputy Foreign Minister for Legal and International Affairs, stated on social media platform X.
Firmly rejecting statements recently delivered by Emirati officials at the United Nations General Assembly, Gharibabadi emphasized: “Emirati officials should, instead of repeating unfounded claims, adhere to the requirements of good neighborliness and the historical and legal realities of the region.”
The senior Iranian diplomat underscored that Tehran considers its territorial integrity and sovereignty over the three strategic Persian Gulf islands non-negotiable. He warned that instrumentalizing international podiums to advance baseless maritime claims serves only as a distraction from genuine regional concerns and undermines multilateral trust.
For decades, Iran has consistently dismissed periodic, orchestrated statements issued by the United Arab Emirates or regional bodies attempting to question Iranian jurisdiction. Iranian officials maintain that sovereignty over Abu Musa, Greater Tunb, and Lesser Tunb is rooted in established international law and an unbroken historical record.
Tehran has reiterated that while it remains committed to diplomacy, de-escalation, and fostering constructive neighborly relations with all littoral states of the Persian Gulf, matters concerning national borders and sovereign territories are absolute red lines. Iran considers any external interference, joint declarations with foreign powers, or calls to refer the domestic status of these islands to international arbitration as invalid, provocative, and contrary to regional security.
The historical facts underpinning Iran’s sovereignty span centuries, extensively documented in regional annals and maritime archives across Europe. During antiquity and through successive Iranian dynasties—including the Safavid, Afsharid, Zand, and Qajar eras—the three islands, alongside the broader maritime expanse of the Persian Gulf, fell under direct Iranian administrative and fiscal control through the ports of Bandar Lengeh and Bushehr.
During the late 19th and early 20th centuries, the British Empire imposed a maritime protectorate over the coastal sheikhdoms—then known as the Trucial States. In pursuit of colonial dominance over the vital sea lines of communication linking India to the West, British colonial authorities unilaterally stationed flags and proxies on the islands, over the continuous, formal objections and diplomatic protests of Tehran.
When Britain announced its withdrawal from east of Suez in 1971, Iran took decisive measures to re-establish and formalize its rightful administration before the formal declaration of the UAE federation. In November 1971, through bilateral arrangements—including the formal Memorandum of Understanding regarding Abu Musa—Iranian sovereign authority was restored. Historic British Admiralty charts, official correspondence from London’s Foreign and Commonwealth Office, and contemporary maritime registries consistently acknowledged Iran’s prior sovereign title, making modern Emirati claims anachronistic attempts to revise colonial history.
Strategic geography: Gatekeepers of the Strait of Hormuz
The three islands occupy an unparalleled geographic position at the western approach to the Strait of Hormuz, the world’s most critical maritime energy chokepoint through which roughly a fifth of global petroleum transit flows.
Greater Tunb and Lesser Tunb sit immediately adjacent to the deep-water shipping lanes utilized by heavy commercial tankers and maritime traffic traversing the Persian Gulf.
Abu Musa, situated slightly further south, commands vital naval surveillance lines and forms the linchpin of defensive depth in the southern waters.
Iran’s presence and defensive readiness across these islands have historically guaranteed freedom of navigation and maritime security against piracy, regional instability, and unilateral foreign adventurism. Tehran views its administration of the islands not merely as a matter of title, but as an essential responsibility for maintaining stability in vital international shipping corridors without reliance on extra-regional powers.
Israel’s shadow in regional waters
Political observers in Tehran point out that Abu Dhabi’s persistent diplomatic agitation over the islands must also be examined through the prism of its broader foreign policy alignments—most notably its normalization of ties with Israel under the so-called Abraham Accords.
By opening the Persian Gulf to intelligence, military, and diplomatic cooperation with Tel Aviv, the UAE has introduced a hostile entity into an inherently sensitive maritime theater. Iranian political and military officials have repeatedly warned against facilitating Israel’s presence in Persian Gulf waters, describing it as a direct threat to collective regional security.
Analysts note that Israel seeks to cultivate leverage on Iran’s immediate southern border, exploiting bilateral frictions to drive a wedge between Muslim-majority neighbors. In this context, recycling stale claims regarding the three Iranian islands is seen by many in Tehran as an attempt to construct artificial disputes, curry favor with Western and Israeli patrons, and justify the growing footprint of destabilizing foreign actors in the Persian Gulf.
Iran has made it clear that while its hand remains extended for genuine regional integration and security cooperation among Persian Gulf states, it will counter any moves that jeopardize its strategic interests, violate its territorial integrity, or pave the way for foreign footholds along its sovereign coastlines.

articles.title: U.S. to send Philippine Coast Guard three spy-equipped planes
articles.body:
- Technology Service Corp. received a $39.6 million contract to supply the Philippine Coast Guard with three pre-owned King Air 350 aircraft by September 2028.
- Two of the aircraft will carry surveillance sensors, and the deal is funded entirely with foreign military sales money.
The United States will supply the Philippine Coast Guard with three secondhand King Air 350 turboprop aircraft, two of them fitted with surveillance sensors, under a $39.6 million contract that finalizes a deal the two countries signed in February.
The U.S. Department of War announced the firm-fixed-price award to Technology Service Corp., a small business based in Arlington, Virginia. The company will provide three pre-owned, extended-range King Air 350 Maritime Domain Awareness aircraft, along with sensor operator training, ferry flights to the Philippines, technical manuals and training materials. Work is scheduled to be completed in September 2028.
The King Air 350 is a twin-engine turboprop built by Textron Aviation’s Beechcraft brand and widely used for patrol, surveillance and medical evacuation. Two of the three aircraft will receive intelligence, surveillance and reconnaissance equipment and mission management software, which lets crews track ships, collect imagery and share what they see. The third will not carry the sensor suite.
An earlier notice from the Naval Air Warfare Center Aircraft Division said all three aircraft would get extended-range fuel tanks, a gross weight increase, Garmin G1000 NXi avionics and high-frequency radios, and that the two surveillance aircraft would carry the King Air 350 Maritime Domain Awareness, or KAMDA, sensor package. Neither notice lists the specific sensors.
The contract is paid for entirely with foreign military sales funds, the money a partner country uses to buy U.S. defense equipment through the U.S. government. All $39.6 million was committed at the time of award. The contract was not competed. The Naval Air Warfare Center Aircraft Division at Patuxent River, Maryland, is managing it.
Most of the work, 70%, will take place in Crystal City, Virginia, with the rest spread across sites in New Century, Meriden and Wichita, Kansas; Manila; Concord, North Carolina; and New Smyrna Beach, Florida.
Philippine Coast Guard Commandant Adm. Ronnie Gil Gavan and U.S. Assistant Secretary of War for Indo-Pacific Security Affairs John Noh signed the letter of offer and acceptance for the aircraft on Feb. 16 in Makati City. At the time, the coast guard said the planes would strengthen its ability to watch Philippine waters and respond faster to emergencies at sea, after the capsizing of the bulk carrier M/V Devon Bay and the January sinking of the ferry M/V Trisha Kerstin 3 off Basilan, which left dozens dead. The coast guard also cited the need for sustained surveillance in the West Philippine Sea, the Philippine name for the parts of the South China Sea it claims.
The two officials also discussed a U.S. Coast Guard search planning program that uses environmental modeling to predict where people lost at sea are likely to be found. This year, the Philippine Coast Guard became the first foreign coast guard to take part in the U.S.-led Rim of the Pacific exercise in Hawaii.

articles.title: British and US forces obliterate target off Scottish coast
articles.body:
Ships, aircraft and a submarine from the United States and the United Kingdom have concluded Exercise Atlantic Thunder 2026 in the North Atlantic, a multi-domain sinking exercise that ended with the destruction of the decommissioned guided missile frigate ex-USS Klakring, according to United States Sixth Fleet, which led it.
Captain Kelechi Ndukwe, commander of Task Force 65, told the UK Defence Journal that the exercise ran from 14 to 25 September, with the sinking itself carried out on 21 September some 150 nautical miles offshore of the Hebrides range. Forces assigned to five American task forces took part, numbered 65, 67, 68, 69 and 1060, alongside the Royal Navy and the United States Air Force.
Asked by this publication what the objectives behind the joint targeting had been, whether they were met, and what an exercise of this kind signals to those who might be watching, Ndukwe said: “We used national technical means to be able to put this together, and I think what it really highlights is the strong bond between the U.S. and the U.K. Our ability to trust each other, to share information, and to show that we are a joint and strong and united force. Peace through strength is really what it shows. Our ability to reach out and touch at the longest distance possible is what we displayed, and you know I think it just shows our ability to be able to work together and interact and really push the limits here.”
In his formal statement on the exercise he put the same argument more bluntly. “Atlantic Thunder demonstrates the unmatched lethality and interoperability of the United States and United Kingdom,” he said. “This sinking exercise not only validated the power behind U.S.-UK offensive weapons but delivers a clear message to adversaries that the U.S. Navy and Royal Navy remain a ready allied force.”
Asked by the UK Defence Journal how much had changed since the previous Atlantic Thunder, held off the same range in 2022, the captain identified reach as the difference. “In past iterations of Atlantic Thunder, we weren’t able to test at the longest range, and I think that’s the biggest change from previous exercises,” he said. “This one, we really were able to test the multi-domain, multi-axis, incorporating the Air Force into it, and really test the boundaries of range for this one, and the new technologies over the past four years that we’re able to bring into play here.”
The guided missile destroyer USS Paul Ignatius demonstrated what Sixth Fleet called the maximum damage and range capability of an anti-surface variant of the Standard Missile 6, and the submarine USS Massachusetts then engaged the target with the Mark 48 Advanced Capability Torpedo, which Sixth Fleet said resulted in the final hit and ultimately sank the frigate. Ndukwe said the sequence had been worked out in advance so the sensors recorded each impact in turn. “We started with the longest range ordnance, which is why we were going with SM-6 first, and then moved in to shorter range,” he said, adding that the SM-6 shot was testing the surface-to-surface engagement at the furthest range available, a figure he said could not be shared.
Britain confirmed both of its newest ship-busting missiles during the same serial, firing the Naval Strike Missile from HMS Portland and Sea Venom from a Wildcat helicopter of 815 Naval Air Squadron. Ndukwe confirmed at the briefing that the Sea Venom shot was the missile’s first live firing since it reached initial operating capability, and that it hit the target.
Lieutenant Commander Louise Kirkaldy, Portland’s principal warfare officer, said: “The successful firing of NSM marks a significant milestone for the Royal Navy, demonstrating our ability to deliver credible, modern maritime strike capability. This achievement reflects the professionalism, dedication and teamwork of all those involved, whose hard work has ensured we remain ready to meet the challenges of today and tomorrow.” Petty Officer James Kenyon, the above water warfare specialist who fired it, called it “the culmination of over a year’s effort in planning and bringing the drills into service.”
No uncrewed systems took part at any stage, the captain confirmed when the question was put to him directly, which sets the exercise apart from much of the trials work now running in British waters.
Four years went into the preparation, involving serving personnel alongside civilian counterparts. On the American side Ndukwe named the portfolio acquisition executive organisation, the Navy Information Warfare Command and the Naval Surface Warfare Center as having worked jointly on it, “ensuring that sensors were properly installed on the frigate to be able to take that data back, inform future capabilities, and really push the envelope on what we’re able to do with future weapons designs.” Sixth Fleet has since said the sensors were placed by Naval Surface Warfare Center Carderock and Naval Information Warfare Center Pacific, and that the data will be used to identify system failures rapidly, determine repair needs and strengthen the navy’s response in a real engagement.
Communications were the part the commander said he was proudest of, and the link architecture was built out by United States Sixth Fleet and run from its headquarters, then shared with HMS Portland, and he said there were no difficulties with it during the exercise. “We were really proud of the ability to communicate throughout the entirety of the exercise,” he said, adding that shared battle damage assessment “will ensure that the Navy and our navies will continue to be capable and lethal fighting forces.”
The units involved covered Paul Ignatius, Massachusetts, HMS Portland, P-8 maritime patrol aircraft flown by both the United States Navy and the Royal Air Force, a Royal Navy Wildcat helicopter, United States Air Force F-15E Strike Eagles, and personnel from Explosive Ordnance Disposal Mobile Unit 8.
On why an American hull was brought across the Atlantic rather than a British one used, Ndukwe described a cost-sharing arrangement between the two governments. “That was part of the agreement between the two navies and the departments of defense, was that we would pay for the tow of the ship across, and then the Royal Navy or the UK would pay for the range,” he said. Klakring entered service on 20 August 1983 and was decommissioned on 22 March 2013, and was named for Rear Admiral Thomas B. Klakring, who won three Navy Crosses commanding the submarine USS Guardfish in the Second World War, as we reported.
What remains of her will stay on the seabed off the Hebrides. “For the environmental side, it was all done during the course of the planning. It was approved by the EPA in advance, and it’ll become a natural reef. It’s sunk in a deep, deep valley there, right off the Hebrides,” the captain said. Sixth Fleet added that in line with Ministry of Defence environmental policy, monitoring was carried out above and below the surface by trained personnel to reduce the risk of harm to the marine environment and to marine mammals.
North Atlantic weather presented obstacles during the serial, Ndukwe said, though all the primary objectives were met and nothing the team had wanted to test failed. Asked by the UK Defence Journal whether work had begun on a follow-on, he confirmed that it had. “Planning has started with the goal of execution in 2028,” he said.

articles.title: Iran ready for preemptive strikes if threatened
articles.body:
Brigadier General Amir Akraminia, spokesman for the Islamic Republic of Iran Army, made the remarks in response to an al-Alam correspondent's questions about US movements in the region and the possibility of war.
"Certainly the Americans are moving and active in the region. But as for whether a war will actually break out, we in the armed forces and the army of the Islamic Republic of Iran have tried to make maximum use of the opportunity of the ceasefire, update our target bank, optimise our equipment, bring new equipment into our combat organisation, and use the reserves, experiences and lessons of the war period," he said.
"Regarding America, I think the Americans are not in a good position in the region, because their bases have suffered serious damage. Our observations show this, through aerial and satellite imagery and through field observations on the ground. Information tells us that American bases have suffered very serious damage, and most of these bases can no longer even be rebuilt."
He said this has caused serious problems for the US military's logistics and support in the region. Fuel and food supply for America now face problems because their important base, especially the Fifth Fleet base in Bahrain, has suffered serious damage and can no longer be rebuilt. They have been forced to prepare supplies from outside the region, from East Asia and from Diego Garcia base, and from this aspect the Americans have faced many difficulties and problems.
On morale, he said some US soldiers have committed suicide and that US forces are not in a good psychological state. "Our overall analysis is that the current situation for America is not a favourable one. From this aspect, the Americans may want to create a change to alter this situation and may commit an act of aggression."
But, he said, the reality is that they have no clear strategy.
On Iran's military strategy after the 12-day war and the concept of preemptive war, Akraminia said the UN Charter prohibits the use of force except in legitimate self-defence. "After the 12-day war, we advanced our strategy toward preemptive war."
He said the martyred Brigadier General Seyyed Abdolrahim Mousavi seriously pursued the strategy that Iran's military doctrine should move from defence to offense. "In this war we practically operationalised this strategy, where we targeted the positions of anti-revolutionary and separatist groups in Iraq's Kurdistan region."
He said that as the US president had announced, large quantities of weapons had been provided to separatists and anti-Iran groups so that, in parallel with the American attack, Iran's land borders in the west would also be attacked.
"This is in fact a kind of preemptive war. Before the enemy could commit aggression, it was targeted. And you have seen that until today, the anti-revolutionaries have not been able to carry out any operation against our land borders."
MNA

articles.title: Iran's Revolutionary Guards call Trump a 'big liar'
articles.body:
Iran's Revolutionary Guards woo US voters with open letter
DUBAI, Sept 29 - Iran's Revolutionary Guards, whose power and influence have expanded since the US and Israel pursued war against Iran, have appealed to US midterm voters to reject President Donald Trump's policies and accept an offer of peaceful coexistence.
The assertions were made on Tuesday in a 25-page open letter addressed to the American people, urging them to oppose US support for Israel and foreign wars and arguing that Iran and the US could coexist if US policy changed.
The letter accused Trump of concealing the peaceful nature of Iran's nuclear programme, which Israel in particular sees as an existential threat, and the effectiveness of Tehran's blockade of Gulf oil.
IRGC spokesperson Hossein Mohebbi told reporters he did not expect the letter to affect the US administration's behaviour some five weeks before the elections, but that voters might hear the message.
"The American people are not knowledgeable about many developments. We believe if they knew more, they would think differently and take other decisions," he said.
IRAN'S GUARDS SAY TRUMP IS NOT TO BE TRUSTED
Among his reasons for waging war on Iran, Trump, whose Republican party is under pressure from the Democrats in opinion polls, has cited the need to ensure that it will never be able to build a nuclear weapon. Last week, he told the UN General Assembly he could "annihilate" the Islamic Republic if he chose.
"The enemy (US) knows that Iran is not after nuclear weapons," Mohebbi said.
"America’s national security and the lives of its service members are entrusted to someone who is not only an inveterate liar but is also an insanely avaricious man whose only motivation in life is the accumulation of greater wealth."
Mohebbi also challenged US assertions that Iran has lost most of its leverage over the Strait of Hormuz, in part because the US military has been able to protect some of the tankers bringing oil out of the Gulf.
"The fact that the Americans might manage, at great expense, considerable trouble and high risk to sneak a small vessel through the Strait of Hormuz under cover of darkness to export, say, 100 or 200 barrels of oil does not mean the Strait is open," Mohebbi said.
According to Kpler data, September has seen a recovery of oil exports via the Strait of Hormuz, which are set to hit almost 10 million barrels per day, about half the pre-war volume. REUTERS

articles.title: NATO sets out plan to make allied forces quantum ready
articles.body:
NATO has published a public summary of a quantum technology roadmap intended to speed up the adoption of quantum computing, communication and sensing across the alliance and allied armed forces, and to guard against the disruption those technologies could cause in the hands of others, according to NATO.
Allies approved the roadmap on 30 July, with the summary released on Tuesday. It builds on the alliance’s Quantum Strategy of 2023 and concentrates on the three branches of the field, alongside how each interacts with other dual-use technologies including artificial intelligence, space and next generation communication networks.
Delivery runs through the Transatlantic Quantum Community and its industry network, working with industry and academia. That body met in Washington on 24 and 25 September, where according to NATO the discussion covered how advances in quantum computing could affect secure communications, critical infrastructure, intelligence, strategic stability and decision making in a crisis, along with what the convergence of artificial intelligence and quantum means for defence.
The same meeting looked at positioning, navigation and timing, and at sensing, in light of the Questor 26 experimentation campaign run earlier this month at La Spezia by the NATO Centre for Maritime Research and Experimentation together with the industry network.
A sufficiently capable quantum computer would break the public key cryptography that protects most military and civil communications, which is why encrypted traffic intercepted today is worth storing against the day it can be read, and why allied governments have been migrating towards post-quantum algorithms. Quantum sensing runs the other way, offering navigation that does not depend on satellite signals at all, which matters a great deal to forces operating where those signals are jammed or spoofed as a matter of routine, as they now are across the Baltic and the Black Sea.
The Transatlantic Quantum Community welcomed Belgium and Bulgaria at the Washington meeting, bringing it to 24 allies alongside six partner nations. The Netherlands took the chair in May for a year with Canada as vice-chair, and the body, established in 2024, is an informal and non-binding grouping of experts drawn from national governments, industry, academia, funding bodies and research institutions rather than a decision-making forum.
Britain has been working the same ground nationally for some years, and the Ministry of Defence and the Defence Science and Technology Laboratory have run quantum navigation trials at sea and in the air over recent years, and the National Quantum Strategy commits public funding across the decade with defence as one of the intended beneficiaries. The Royal Navy’s experimentation vessel XV Patrick Blackett has been used for trials of this kind.
The full roadmap summary is published on the NATO site alongside the announcement, and the alliance gives no figures for what the work will cost or timescales for when any of the capability is expected to reach the field.

articles.title: Iran awaits US response to proposal as Trump denies concessions
articles.body:
Breadcrumb
Iran waits for US response to peace proposals as Trump denies making concessions
Iran put forward ideas for reaching a new peace agreement with the US through Qatari mediators, Iranian state media reported on Monday, while US President Donald Trump denied reports that he had offered Tehran concessions to end the war.
Iranian Foreign Minister Abbas Araghchi is currently in New York, where he has discussed a number of ideas with Qatari mediators to be presented to the US. He denied reports that Tehran had shown flexibility on the nuclear issue.
On Tuesday, Qatari Foreign Ministry spokesperson Majed Al-Ansari said efforts were still underway to arrange meetings between the US and Iran.
“We are carrying messages between the parties to build common ground,” he said.
Al-Ansari, however, warned against Iranian threats to target infrastructure in Gulf countries, saying: “Iranian attacks on our countries are unjustified aggression, and we did not choose to be a party to this war.”
He added that “any threat to infrastructure is a violation of the principles of international law and good-neighbourly relations.”
Araghchi said a seven-point plan had been conveyed to the US through Qatari mediators, adding that Iran was still waiting for an official response despite Trump’s statements.
Following a report by Axios that Trump was prepared to ease sanctions on Iran and release frozen funds in exchange for concrete steps regarding Iran’s nuclear programme, the US president angrily denied the claim.
“This is untrue. I offered them NOTHING,” he wrote on his Truth Social platform on Monday.
Araghchi added that Iranian officials met one of the Qatari mediators on Monday and discussed ideas for paving the way towards implementing Iran’s conditions. He said the mediators would present the ideas to the US side before conveying Washington’s final response to Tehran.
Araghchi expressed hope that the US response would arrive on Tuesday, adding that he would leave New York for Tehran within hours and that Qatari mediators would know how to deliver the response as soon as they received it.
The Iranian foreign minister added that Iran’s position on its nuclear programme remained unchanged and that Tehran had shown no flexibility on the issue.
He said the current discussions were limited to the Strait of Hormuz and that the strategic waterway would only be reopened if a series of conditions communicated by Iran were met.
According to officials who spoke to the Associated Press, the proposal currently under discussion involves reopening the Strait of Hormuz and lifting the US blockade on Iranian ports, followed by the lifting of sanctions on Iran.
A draft of the agreement indicates that the strait would be reopened under a separate understanding discussed between Iran and Oman, with no fees imposed on ships. The agreement would temporarily regulate the movement of vessels through the strategic waterway.

articles.title: Iran embassy rejects UK media claims over RAF Fairford arrests, warns against fueling ‘Iranophobia’
articles.body:
Iran embassy rejects UK media claims over RAF Fairford arrests, warns against fueling ‘Iranophobia’
TEHRAN – The Embassy of the Islamic Republic of Iran in London has categorically rejected attempts by British media to implicate the country in the recent arrest of five individuals near the Royal Air Force (RAF) Fairford base, labeling the speculation as “fabricated” and “malicious.”
The embassy statement, released on the social media platform X, firmly condemned the narrative being pushed by certain British outlets, warning that such baseless accusations serve only to exacerbate anti-Iranian sentiment within the United Kingdom.
“The Embassy of the Islamic Republic of Iran in London categorically rejects and strongly condemns the recent unfounded and malicious speculations published by some British individuals and media outlets attempting to link Iran to arrest of five suspects in the vicinity of RAF Fairford base,” the embassy said on X.
“The circulation of such fabricated speculations, particularly in the aftermath of the criminal acts of aggression committed by the United States and the Israeli regime against the Iranian people, will serve no purpose other than to fuel Iranophobia propaganda in the UK,” it added.
The mission further emphasized that it “reserves the right to take appropriate legal measures, as necessary, to safeguard the rights and interests of the country and its people in response to misleading and damaging media narratives.”
The arrests occurred near RAF Fairford, a facility that has long drawn scrutiny from Tehran due to its role in hosting US bombers potentially deployed for regional operations. Counterterrorism police identified the five suspects as British nationals, aged 23 to 25, all residents of inner London—specifically from Camden, Westminster, and Willesden. The individuals are currently being held on suspicion of preparing terrorist acts and offenses under the Explosives Act.
Despite the fact that the suspects are UK citizens, political rhetoric in Britain has attempted to cast the incident through a geopolitical lens. UK Foreign Secretary Ed Miliband, speaking at the Labour Party conference in Liverpool, claimed the incident served as “a reminder of the threats our country faces,” and provocatively stated, “We will act against the proxies of Iran.”
Miliband refused to elaborate on the investigation or address claims made by US President Donald Trump, who suggested the suspects had been under surveillance by American intelligence for an extended period. When questioned by reporters regarding a potential Iranian connection, Trump did not offer a direct denial, instead opting for a vague gesture.
Tehran has consistently maintained that the use of British bases for hostile actions against the Iranian people is a provocative stance that jeopardizes regional security.
