articles.title: Iranians stagger under soaring costs of seven months of war
articles.body:
Iranians stagger under soaring costs of seven months of war
LONDON, Sept 29 - Iran's leaders may radiate bullishness in their war with the United States, but life is becoming ever tougher for ordinary citizens unable to afford basic necessities or rent as a US blockade cuts the state's financial lifeline - oil exports.
From an engineer forced out of Tehran by high rent to a woman forced to stop smoking because of the price of cigarettes and carers struggling to buy medicines, all areas of daily life are affected.
"I'm forced to sell my items with a very small and negligible profit, yet I can't close my business because then I'd be unemployed," said Behnam Riazi, a restaurant owner interviewed on camera in Tehran.
Riazi cannot raise his prices because his customers cannot pay more - any most anyway buy only necessities now.
How far economic strains may push Iran towards diplomatic compromise is unclear, as it tightens its own stranglehold on Gulf energy exports through the Strait of Hormuz, driving up oil and gas prices in the US and around the world.
ECONOMIC MISERY MAY SPUR DIPLOMACY
However, the latest burst of diplomacy was partly spurred by economic strains, US, Middle Eastern and Iranian sources said last week. Iranian officials have repeatedly expressed fears of unrest, and cracked down ruthlessly on rumblings of dissent.
In January, over a month before the US and Israel began their war on Iran, authorities killed thousands of demonstrators exasperated by years of cumulative economic distress.
But now, all those Reuters spoke to said they had too many daily worries to think about protesting.
Hediyeh, a housewife in her 60s in northern Iran, survives on her husband's civil service pension. She can barely afford medicine or even the adult diapers needed by her elderly mother, who has Alzheimer's disease.She wanted to buy her grandson a new bag for his first day at school this autumn, but it cost five or six times what she had expected, and in the end she could only buy him a notebook and pencils.
Like most of the Iranians Reuters interviewed by phone or messaging app, she did not want to be identified, fearing punishment for speaking to foreign media.
A.J., a teacher who asked only to be identified by his initials, also said he cannot always afford the medicine his mother needs.
He has already moved in with his mother and siblings in a northern village, leaving Tehran after schools moved online because of the war, but fears he will no longer be able to afford to return if in-person teaching resumes.
In Sanandaj, capital of Kurdistan province, 34-year-old psychotherapist Nazanin has given up smoking because of the cost after having previously found it impossible to do so, she said.
Those who can afford to bypass the usual ways of obtaining goods or services through the black market are finding it has become more pervasive, though the cost has gone up.
One man said he had paid $200 in hard currency to a surgeon to get around the bureaucratic process needed for an operation.
Another said police requests for bribes were growing more frequent, and that he had had to pay more than before after being stopped at a checkpoint without identification papers.
JOBS BEING CUT IN PRIVATE SECTOR
An architect, who only gave his initials A.A., said even wealthier Iranians were cutting back: "All of them have become poor relative to the lifestyle they used to have."
His car had a puncture last week and he is having to drive on a spare tyre for the two weeks it takes to get a cheap replacement; he can no longer afford those available immediately.
He worries that Iran is heading for fuel shortages, which could disrupt supply chains and cause wider economic havoc.
Already, the war is causing heavy job losses across the private sector.
M.H., a woman in Tehran who also asked to be identified only by her initials, said she had lost her job this month in the procurement department of a local business even though her one-year contract had only been renewed the previous day.
She now has to return the money the company had paid into Iran's social security system for the coming year. Her family has strictly prioritised spending, with food at the top.
"Thank goodness we can still afford the internet, so we can stay connected online, maybe watch a film," she said.
Bijan, 40, a former engineer who now offers tuition to students to make money, said he and his wife had left their Tehran flat and moved to an area he described as "half slum" outside the capital.
The couple have exhausted their savings and plan to move to another city where they hope to live more cheaply.
Shop owners see the slide in living standards better than most. Ramin Yousefnia said in an on-camera interview in Tehran that all the customers in his grocery shop had cut down.
"Something they used to buy five or 10 of, they can only buy two of now," he said. "Don't even get me started on savings. This is the reality." REUTERS

articles.title: US sanctions 10 international entities over allegedly procuring weapons for Iran's Defense Ministry
articles.body:
The United States has sanctioned 10 individuals and entities, including some based in China, Hong Kong and Pakistan, for helping Iran's Defense Ministry procure weapons and components, the US Treasury Department said Tuesday.
The sanctions are part of a broader push by the Trump administration to isolate Iran economically and force it to negotiate an end to the US-Iran war that began in February.
“Under Operation Economic Outcast, Treasury will continue to target and disrupt those who provide material, technological, or financial support that allows the Iranian regime to sustain its terrorist enterprise,” US Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent said.
“Treasury will not tolerate any support to the regime and will continue to identify, expose, and isolate Iran’s enablers.”
The US Treasury said the sanctions were aimed at degrading Tehran's ability to reconstitute its weapons programs, while increasing the costs for those who supported its procurement efforts.
Iraqi Airways to resume Iran flights in October after securing US exemption
Iraqi Airways is preparing to resume flights to Iran in October, Iraq's transport ministry said Tuesday, after suspending flights amid US sanctions restricting services to Iranian airlines.
The ministry said Iraq had secured a special exemption allowing Iraqi Airways to operate services to Iran.
Iraq halted flights to and from Iran on Friday in line with US sanctions, and the government had sought exemptions for travel related to pilgrimage, medical treatment and education.
The transport ministry said services next month would initially operate from the Shi'ite holy city of Najaf once regulatory and technical requirements were completed.
A source in the Iraqi transport ministry said the US Treasury Department provided the exemption, and it would run for one month. The source said the number of allowed flights has not yet been determined.

articles.title: World News in Brief: Deadly Myanmar strikes as Malaysia begins deportations, new emergency funding released, Gaza and West Bank update
articles.body:
World News in Brief: Deadly Myanmar strikes as Malaysia begins deportations, new emergency funding released, Gaza and West Bank update
The UN chief on Tuesday strongly condemned an airstrike that reportedly killed at least 50 people at a market in Myanmar’s Rakhine state and called for those responsible to be held to account.
Forces from the military junta reportedly hit Kyauktaw township around midday on Monday, when the market’s more than 200 shops were busy with vendors, customers and transport workers
Women and children were among the dead and at least 58 people were injured, many critically. The toll is expected to rise.
UN human rights chief Volker Türk said the attack raised serious concerns about respect for international humanitarian law, describing Myanmar as a country “wracked by extreme violence”.
He highlighted abuses against the Rohingya in particular by both the army and the opposition Arakan Army armed group.
Malaysia urged to stop deportations
The strike came hours before Malaysia began implementing a plan to deport some 5,000 Myanmar nationals.
The plan follows a reported agreement between Myanmar’s military rulers and Kuala Lumpur, which Malaysia has said would involve only voluntary repatriations.
The UN refugee agency, UNHCR, says it has not been involved in identifying those being returned, who have reportedly been held in detention centres.
Mr. Türk urged the authorities to halt the process immediately, warning that conditions in Myanmar are “far from safe and sustainable”.
The UN chief echoed that call over the reported return of some 1,500 people, with UNHCR stressing that no one should be sent back to a place where they risk persecution or torture, and that continuing violence in Rakhine shows conditions do not exist for safe, voluntary returns.
Fletcher unlocks funds ahead of El Niño-driven drought in Africa
UN relief chief Tom Fletcher has released millions of dollars from the Central Emergency Response Fund (CERF) to get ahead of the worst impacts of El Niño-driven drought in South Sudan, Zimbabwe and Chad.
In South Sudan, where more than two in every three people – over 10 million in total – already need aid, $6 million will support early action on a worsening drought that Mr. Fletcher warned is putting lives and livelihoods at risk.
The funds will help provide food, health, nutrition, protection, water and sanitation services.
In Zimbabwe, $4 million will be used for anticipatory action to get food, health and nutrition support in place before the drought arrives.
In Chad, $3.6 million will help 350,000 people prepare for dry conditions that could worsen food insecurity and undermine livelihoods.
Best laid plans
The funds were released automatically once trigger thresholds were met, bringing anticipatory action funding for the drought in seven different regions of Chad to $8 million since the start of the year.
The funds will complement the Chadian government’s efforts and support early warning, cash assistance for vulnerable households, livestock feed, malnutrition screening and treatment, disease surveillance and the prevention and treatment of gender-based violence.
The UN has set up a Global Emergency Fund to help people in crises around the world. You can donate here.
Israeli fire near UN sites in Gaza as settler attacks continue in West Bank
Israeli fire was reported near UN facilities and humanitarian convoys in Gaza on several occasions in recent days, according to the UN humanitarian office (OCHA) on Tuesday.
No casualties have been reported, but the UN stressed that civilians – including aid workers and humanitarian operations – must always be protected.
Aid work continues. In the third week of September, protection partners gave around 13,000 Gazans mental health support, counselling and other services.
They also distributed around 740 food parcels, 6,000 adult diapers and 2,000 assistive devices including wheelchairs, as well as hygiene kits for more than 200 displaced families.
The UN agency for Palestine refugees, UNRWA, says 1,394 Palestinians have been killed since the faltering October 2025 ceasefire, citing local health authorities, and that some 94 per cent of the population need shelter assistance.
West Bank attacks
Settler attacks continue to undermine Palestinians’ safety and livelihoods, OCHA says, adding to pressure on people to leave their homes. Several houses were damaged in the village of Jalud, in Nablus governorate, on Monday night.
Over the weekend in Tubas governorate, a water network serving Palestinians was vandalised and vehicles carrying water and produce were seized.
News reports said more than 100 settlers attacked Jalud, stopping the al-Tubasi family from returning to homes that settlers had seized weeks earlier.
The family was reportedly escorted by Israeli forces after Israel’s High Court ruled earlier this month that they must be allowed back.
Two of their houses were set on fire and Israeli security forces were also targeted, according to news reports.
OCHA has recorded more than 1,600 settler attacks this year – an average of 6.7 a day, up from five a day in 2025 – and more than 4,300 Palestinians have been displaced.

articles.title: Russia strikes 2 Kiev data centers, missile depot in overnight attack
articles.body:
MOSCOW, Sept. 29 (Xinhua) -- Russian forces struck the Bi-mobile and Parkovyi data centers in Kiev and a locomotive depot housing a warehouse of FP-5 Flamingo missiles in overnight attacks, the Russian Defense Ministry said Tuesday.
The Belogorodka warehouse terminal used for the production and storage of drones was also struck in the Kiev region, the ministry said. In the Odesa region, strikes targeted the Usatovo electrical substation supplying power to Ukrainian port infrastructure and a drone production workshop in Velikodolinskoye.
On the maritime front, infrastructure used to unload military cargo was struck at the port of Izmail. At the port of Odesa, a dry cargo ship carrying military equipment was hit, while another vessel was struck while en route to the port, the ministry said.
In a separate statement, the ministry said Russian forces intercepted 129 Ukrainian drones across multiple regions overnight. ■

articles.title: AI risks ‘spiraling out of control’ – Nobel-winning group chief
articles.body:
AI risks ‘spiraling out of control’ – Nobel-winning group chief
Artificial intelligence could develop beyond human control unless governments and private companies work together to establish safeguards, the head of the Nobel Peace Prize-winning Pugwash Conferences on Science and World Affairs, Karen Hallberg, has told RT.
Speaking at the Valdai Discussion Club outside of Moscow on Tuesday, Hallberg compared AI with nuclear technology, saying both can bring major benefits while also posing serious dangers.
“AI is also a dual-use technology because AI has brought a lot of benefit for humanity,” she said, citing the technology’s use in medicine and everyday life.
However, she warned that AI capable of recursively improving itself could develop in unpredictable ways. “We have to really listen to the experts of these big corporations when they say that this is already happening – spiraling out of control,” Hallberg said.
Governments must work directly with companies developing AI to establish common rules, she added, noting that unlike during the early nuclear era, much of the technology is being developed by private corporations.
“The human being has to have total control,” Hallberg said, calling for safeguards to be built into AI algorithms.
Warnings over the potential consequences of increasingly powerful AI have also come from the companies developing it. US firm Anthropic, which is expected to go public as early as mid-October, has warned prospective investors that advanced AI could pose “catastrophic or existential risks to humanity.” According to Reuters, around 80 pages of its 261-page IPO prospectus are devoted to risk factors.
Pugwash brings together scientists and public figures seeking to reduce threats from armed conflict and weapons of mass destruction. The organization was jointly awarded the Nobel Peace Prize in 1995 with its co-founder Joseph Rotblat.

articles.title: Senior Gaza resistance commander Abu Hamza martyred in dawn raid
articles.body:
Senior Gaza resistance commander Abu Hamza martyred in dawn raid
TEHRAN — The Izz al-Din al-Qassam Brigades, Hamas’ military wing, confirmed the martyrdom of senior commander Izz al-Din Abdul Aziz al-Beik, known as Abu Hamza, following a targeted Israeli one-way attack drone strike in Gaza City early Tuesday.
The dawn raid struck an apartment inside the Al-Batoul building in the Al-Nasr neighborhood, killing Abu Hamza alongside fellow fighter Muhannad Abu Foul and wounding several civilians, including children. The blast ignited a fire that completely destroyed the home.
As a member of al-Qassam’s General Military Council, Abu Hamza led the Northern Gaza Brigade, having assumed command after the martyrdom of Ahmed al-Ghandour.
Abu Hamza leaves behind a formidable record of frontline service.
According to the Al-Qassam Brigades’ statement, he commanded the first special unit in northern Gaza during the Al-Aqsa Intifada, led the Imad Aql Battalion in 2009, and directed military intelligence for the northern brigade starting in 2015.
